#6534. Why Did Early Humans Collect Strange Stones 500,000 Years Ago? Scientists Have a New Theory

Prehistoric discoveries in Israel raise the possibility that keeping meaningful objects helped early humans distinguish personal memories from stories and gradually develop a sense of identity.

A stone picked up during a hike or a seashell brought home from the beach might seem ordinary to everyone else. Yet years later, that small object can bring back memories of where you were, who you were with, and what made the experience special. It’s a familiar human habit, and researchers now believe its origins may reach back nearly half a million years.

A new study from Tel Aviv University suggests that early humans may have collected and kept objects for much the same reason we do today. The researchers propose that these prehistoric keepsakes could have helped shape our ability to remember personal experiences and develop a sense of who we are.

The idea emerged from archaeological discoveries at several prehistoric sites in Israel, where researchers found colorful stones, unusual handaxes, and much older tools that appeared to have been collected despite offering no obvious practical benefit.

At Qesem Cave, for example, small, colorful pebbles had been brought in from different locations. In the Sakhnin Valley, handaxes were made from flint containing fossils or unusual geological patterns. Some were carefully shaped so that these distinctive features remained at the center, where they could be seen and touched.

Other discoveries offer an intriguing connection to the past. At Revadim, Jaljulia, and Qesem Cave, researchers identified older flint tools that had apparently been collected after their surfaces had changed with age. Although some were resharpened, much of their original surfaces and evidence of earlier workmanship remained intact.

Why would someone keep an old tool when they could make a new one? The researchers suggest that its age and appearance may have been part of its appeal. Just as an old family heirloom can carry meaning beyond its usefulness, these objects might have been valued for the experiences or histories associated with them.

Dr. Yoav Ram of Tel Aviv University’s School of Zoology explains the possibility:

“When early humans brought a colorful stone or an old tool they had found in the landscape back to their cave, that object may have helped them remember a significant event or encounter for the rest of their lives. In this way, keepsakes may have become a kind of ‘external memory device,’ supporting the evolution of brain mechanisms responsible for autobiographical memory, which is so characteristic of us as humans and so important in shaping our identity.”

There may be a deeper psychological reason why such objects mattered. Our minds do not simply store experiences. They must also distinguish between things we personally experienced, stories we heard from others, and events we imagined.

The researchers propose that seeing or touching a familiar object could have helped early humans make those distinctions. A stone collected from a particular location, for instance, might have brought back a personal memory of being there.

That ability could have mattered well beyond individual recollection. Remembering encounters, alliances, gifts, mutual obligations, and rights connected to particular places helps people maintain relationships and cooperate. A keepsake could also be carried elsewhere and shown to others, potentially making a personal account more convincing and helping establish trust.

The researchers believe this behavior may have become especially useful as early humans faced changes in their environment.

Prof. Ran Barkai offers one possible explanation:

“The disappearance of large animals, particularly elephants, required early humans to develop new hunting methods and become familiar with hunting grounds inhabited by animals such as fallow deer and wild cattle. Objects taken from these places may have helped them maintain a personal connection with the places that would henceforth provide their livelihood.”

Over many generations, the researchers suggest, keeping meaningful objects may have placed evolutionary pressure on the brain systems involved in identifying where memories come from and how reliable they are.

In this proposed scenario, objects and memory evolved together. As people increasingly used physical reminders of their experiences, the brain mechanisms supporting personal memory may have become more sophisticated.

That process could have contributed to the development of autobiographical memory, our ability to connect individual experiences into a continuing story of our lives. It is an important part of how we understand our identities and our relationships with others.

The researchers emphasize that their interpretation remains a hypothesis. An unusual stone or carefully preserved tool does not necessarily prove that its owner associated it with a personal memory. The archaeological evidence cannot reveal exactly what someone was thinking hundreds of thousands of years ago.

However, the findings suggest that the habit of keeping meaningful objects may date back roughly 500,000 years, long before written records or photographs.

And if the researchers’ interpretation is correct, the simple act of keeping a stone from a memorable place may once have played a role in the evolution of how humans remember their lives.

Reference: “Homo Memorabiliaxis: Souvenirs and the Evolution of Autobiographical Memory and Self” by Ran Barkai, Ella Assaf, Bar Efrati, Tal Simon, Liad Mudrik and Yoav Ram, 19 October 2026, Evolutionary Anthropology: Issues, News, and Reviews. DOI: 10.1002/evan.70051

#6533. Extremely Accurate Measurements of a Pair of Flaring Red Dwarfs

About 59 light years away, a binary pair of red dwarfs are orbiting a common center of gravity. Unlike stars like our Sun, which are relatively radio-quiet, red dwarfs (M dwarfs) can produce strong radio emissions. A team of astronomers used that to their advantage to take precision measurements of a binary pair of M dwarfs about 59 million light years from Earth. They determined the stars' orbits and masses with uncommon accuracy.

One fundamental fact about low and intermediate mass stars, including M dwarfs, is that they rotate more rapidly when they're younger. Stars inherit angular momentum from their formation in gas clouds, and since M dwarfs are so small, that momentum is concentrated, making them spin rapidly. They eventually slow down, but this initial rapid rotation makes them very active.

The fast rotation generates powerful magnetic dynamos, and young M dwarfs exhibit very large sunspots and more frequent, powerful stellar flares.

One subset of young M dwarfs is even more extreme. They're called Complex Periodic Variable (CPV) stars, and they're very young, between about 10 and 100 million years old. They're M dwarfs that display complex, periodical optical light curves with sharp drops rather than smooth drops found in most stellar light curves. Their drops aren't simple; there can be multiple dips and peaks during a single rotation. Astrophysicists call their light curves multi-harmonic, and the patterns repeat across multiple rotations.

This image shows CPV light curves for three typical CPV stars found by TESS. Notice the sharp drops in the curves rather than typical smooth drops found in other stellar light curves. Image Credit: Bouma et al. 2023. AnJ

The binary system in this research is named DG CVn, and one of them is a CPV star. Though CPV stars have complex light curves generated by their youthful, rapid rotation, their youthfulness also means they're radio loud. In fact, since both of these stars are young M dwarfs, they're both radio loud. That helped the researchers measure them with such accuracy.

The measurments of DG CVn are in new research in Astronomy and Astrophysics titled "Accurate dynamical mass and orbit determination of the M dwarf binary DG CVn using astrometric very long baseline interferometry." The lead author is Paul VLBI , a network system engineer at the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry ERIC (JIVE), and a Leiden Observatory PhD student. It's noteworthy that this is the first mass measurement of a system with a CPV star.

"We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star." - Boven et al. 2026.

The astronomers' results are based on observations that spanned 18 years. Observations with the National Science Foundationâs Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) between 2023 and 2025 were especially important in their precise results. The VLBA is a system of 10 radiotelescopes across the USA, each one measuring 25 meters. The 10 dishes work as an interferometer, and the VLBA has the longest baseline in the world, up to 8,611 km long.

"Astrometry through very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) allows the monitoring of radio-loud stars and the detection of any reflex motion due to stellar or substellar companions," the authors write. Reflex motion is the characteristic gravitational wobble induced in a star when a companion tugs on it.

That wobble is often used to detect unseeable exoplanets orbiting stars. Even a small planet can make its star wobble, and that's at the heart of the radial velocity method of detecting exoplanet. The DG CVn system was actually found when astronomers were searching for exoplanets with the radial velocity method. But the system exhibited a more powerful and complex wobble than an exoplanet would.

âWe were really lucky to hear about this object when we had developed tools with which we could explain these motions,â said Boven. âBut the real surprise came when we also detected the second radio-loud dwarf in the observations we did to confirm our model. It really allowed us to measure the system very precisely.â

Measuring reflex motion accurately with the VLBI let the astronomers track the stars' paths, including the tiny wobbles, which in turn let them understand the mass of the stars with extreme precision.

This figure from the research shows the VLBI detections of both members of DG CVn, and their modeled motion across the sky. The dates mark the predicted positions of DG CVn B over time. The inset image shows recent observations when both sources were detected. Image Credit: Boven et al. 2026. A&A.

"In our recent observations, we reliably detected both binary components," the authors write. "A unique and accurate determination of the 1647.647 Â± 0.027 day orbit, with a parallax distance of 18.1851 Â± 0.0033 pc (about 59 light years), is presented. The dynamical masses were estimated with a precision of 0.16% from the sampled posteriors."

The pair of stars orbit each other every 4.511 years on an elongated elliptical orbit. When they're closest to one another, they're only separated by 0.59 astronomical units. DG CVn A is the more massive of the pair with 0.39 solar masses, while DG CVn B has 0.36 solar masses. The pair is close enough to measure their distance with parallax, which gives accurate measurements.

The red dwarfs and their radio emissions are central to this work. The stars are simply too close together from this distance to be separated in optical observations. But the VLBA can pinpoint their locations with extreme accuracy. All of this work let the researchers characterize the system in clear detail, following the motions of both stars through the sky separately.

âDG CVn is a beautiful example of what precise radio astrometry can reveal,â said Jay Blanchard, NSF National Radio Astronomy Observatory astronomer and study co-author. âBy following these two stars over many years, we can see their orbital motion directly and use that motion to determine properties that would otherwise be extremely difficult to measure.â

These accurate measurements also tell astronomers about their planetary systems. Planets form in protoplanetary disks around stars, and since these stars are so close together, that limits the size of their disks. Smaller disks mean smaller planets, so that limits the size of any exoplanets in the system. It's also extremely unlikely that any long-period planets are orbiting either star.

According to the researchers' estimates, an exoplanet in orbit around one of the stars could only be in a stable orbit if its orbital period was less than approximately 23 days. For a circumbinary planet orbiting both stars, the orbital period would have to be at least about 36 years. These approximations are also important, because they can refine the understanding of how exoplanets can form and survive in binary star systems.

Gaia's Data Release 4 is due in a couple of weeks, and it will include binary star parameters for the mission's complete survey. But that data alone won't be able to differentiate between binaries where both are low mass stars, and binaries where one might be a massive planet. But the VLBI will be able to address that. "Astrometric follow-up of selected detections with VLBI can help to differentiate between binary star systems and reflex motion due to large exoplanets (or even both)," the authors write.

"We have presented a complete binary orbital solution with high accuracy based on VLBI astrometry of a binary that is difficult to resolve for optical telescopes on the ground or in orbit," the authors write. "The absolute astrometry provided by VLBI allowed the individual dynamical masses to be determined with high accuracy. These results show that VLBI is well suited for studying the orbits of radio-loud stars."

The results also show how powerful the combination of archival observations and new observations can be. "The value of combining archival and recent VLBI astrometric observations has been demonstrated. It resulted in a highly accurate determination of the system composition, orbit, position, and distance," the authors write. "We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star."

The VLBI network of radio dishes is about to have a growth spurt when the Square Kilometre Array and the Next Generation Very Large Array come online. That will improve the system's reach and precision.

"In the future, we hope to make measurements precise enough to detect planets in orbit around such radio-loud dwarfs,â said Huib van Langevelde, chief scientist a the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry and Leiden Observatory professor. âWe think that when the ngVLA and the SKA become part of the VLBI network, we can do even more precise measurements, for many more, more distant stars.â

#6532. 7 Simple Steps for Winterizing Your Lawn Mower

You can’t just park it in the shed and forget it. Both gas-powered and cordless mowers need to be prepared for winter storage.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Somehow the end of the year is upon us and mowing season is winding down. And while you should still be mowing your lawn until the first hard frost hits, soon it’ll be time to retire it for the winter, and you get to give that chore a rest for a bit. But you can’t just store the mower in the shed and forget about it. To ensure your lawn mower is ready to go next season, you need to winterize it before sending it into hibernation.

Winterizing is especially important for gas-powered mowers, which have engines that need fuel, oil, and an air filter to run properly. You should do some light maintenance on them before the cold weather arrives. While cordless electric lawn mowers are easier to maintain, there are still a few steps you should take before storing them away.

Here are our tips for winterizing any lawn mower so it’s ready to go in the spring. Note that you don’t have to do them in this exact order; for example, you might want to leave fuel stabilization until later in the process, but we wanted to keep it at the top, since it’s one of the most important steps.

Prepping your gas-powered lawn mower for winter storage isn’t hard; there are just several things to consider, and if you cover them all, it should only take an hour or so. You will be dealing with engine fluids, however, so choose a work area and clothing that you don’t mind getting dirty.

When left for long periods, gasoline can become “stale,” meaning it evaporates and oxidizes, making it less combustible. It can also create residues that could damage the engine. Also, the ethanol found in most gasoline can break down if left to sit, causing performance issues and attracting water that can cause corrosion (one of the reasons ethanol-free gas is better for lawn mowers).

You can avoid the problems by adding a fuel stabilizer, but if there is any air in the tank, it’s not a perfect solution. Meanwhile, siphoning the gas from the tank is not truly going to remove all of it, so here’s our advice, in steps:

Not everyone will recommend this method, but we believe that, since a full tank has almost no air in it, there is little space for fuel to evaporate or for condensation to form due to temperature changes. Therefore, you are less likely to encounter problems than if you had drained the tank.

Large gas-powered mowers, such as lawn tractors and zero-turn mowers, typically have a battery to power the starter, lights, and other accessories. Gas walk-behind mowers with an electric start feature will also have a battery. It’s a good idea to remove it for the winter and clean it to remove corrosion on the terminals or battery posts. When performing this task, wear nitrile gloves and eye protection. If your battery has a lot of corrosion, you don't want to remove it in a way that it gets airborne. You can use a solution of water and baking soda to neutralize the corrosion and wipe it off with a rag or microfiber cloth.

Most experts recommend replacing your spark plug every year. Changing your spark plug can vary depending on the model of lawn mower you own, so always consult your manual. If you do not feel it’s necessary to replace it, at least remove it to check for any damage. If you see a lot of carbon buildup, rust, or cracks, it’s best to change it.

Drain the oil from the mower after letting it run for 5 minutes—warm oil flows more easily. For walk-behind mowers, this will require you to tip the mower over, so it’s probably better to remove the gas first or at least make sure the gas tank is securely sealed. When tipping the mower, the carburetor and air filter sections should be facing upward to avoid oil contamination—since the oil spout is usually on the opposite side of the carb and filter, you’ll naturally be following this rule anyway. But it’s good advice for when you tip the mower to clean the underside of the deck as well.

This is pretty easy to do, but it helps to know what the filter is made of. Paper and fiber filters should be replaced. If it’s a foam filter element, you can use water and Dawn dish soap, but make sure to rinse it well and let it air dry completely before reinstalling it.

You should be cleaning your mower deck throughout the summer, but if not, make a point to do it before storing it; otherwise, the caked-on grass may cause corrosion or attract bugs and vermin. As mentioned above, make sure to tip your mower so that the air box and carburetor are on the high side to avoid fuel contamination.

After you’ve completed the task of cleaning the deck, it’s a good idea to wipe down your engine with a damp cloth, removing any dirt or debris, and dry it with another towel.

The end of the season is a good time to sharpen your mower blade or replace it altogether. You can take it to a lawn mower repair shop to have it done, but if you have a few basic tools, it’s very simple to do it yourself.

The beauty of a cordless mower is that there’s less maintenance you need to perform. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t steps to take before storing it away for winter.

Batteries are the lifeblood of a cordless mower, so you need to take care of them. Don’t leave them in the mower over winter, especially if you’re keeping it in an uninsulated shed that sees cold temperatures. Remove your batteries and charge them to between 40 and 60 percent. Check the charge level every two months or so, as lithium-ion batteries lose power over time. Partially recharge the batteries if they dip close to 20 percent or lower.

Store your batteries in a cool, dark place such as a basement or insulated garage (but not near a furnace or heat source). For a riding mower that has a built-in battery you cannot remove, park it in a garage or at least a covered area. If stored in a place that gets below freezing, don’t leave it on a charger or try to recharge it, as some batteries (lithium-ion) should not be charged below 32 degrees Fahrenheit. Get it to a warmer place or wait until a warmer day.

This isn’t much different from how you do it for a gas mower; just be careful if using water to do any cleaning, as this can potentially damage electrical components. Also, be sure to remove the batteries before you do any kind of cleaning on a cordless mower.

Again, this isn’t a different process than a gas mower; just make sure the batteries are removed first to avoid the chance of the mower starting up accidentally.

#6530. The Origins of Wealth Inequality May Go Back 5,000 Years, Ancient Graves Reveal

The roots of inherited privilege may reach back thousands of years, with ancient graves revealing how one European community gradually became more divided by wealth and status.

Among nearly 300 prehistoric graves examined in Bohemia, the richest belonged to a young girl. Buried alongside her was an exceptionally rare copper neck ring, an object that raises an intriguing question about life thousands of years ago. Was she born into a wealthy family, or did her elaborate burial reflect something else about how her community valued status?

For archaeologists, questions like these are difficult to answer because prehistoric societies left behind no census records, tax registers, or written accounts of who held wealth and power.

A new archaeological method is helping researchers piece together that missing history by examining how people buried their dead. Developed by University of Copenhagen archaeologist Mikkel Nørtoft during his PhD research, QuantWealth combines multiple forms of archaeological evidence to reconstruct social status, displays of wealth, and inequality. In a study published in the Journal of Neolithic Archaeology, Nørtoft and his colleague Adam B. Rohrlach applied the method to 296 graves belonging to the Corded Ware culture in present-day Bohemia, dating from approximately 2900 to 2300 BCE.

The researchers examined burial practices and grave goods alongside genetic ancestry, Y-chromosome patterns that trace paternal lineages, and skeletal evidence of age, sex, and pathological conditions. By comparing these different clues, they could investigate how social differences changed across several centuries. The findings suggest that inequality developed gradually rather than emerging as a firmly established social hierarchy when migrants from the eastern European steppe settled in the region.

The Corded Ware culture formed part of a much larger transformation in prehistoric Europe, when populations migrating from the steppe helped spread early Indo-European dialects across the continent. Archaeologists have debated whether these newcomers also introduced strongly patriarchal societies in which wealth and power passed primarily through family lines. The evidence from Bohemia points toward a more complicated history.

“Archaeologists have long debated whether steppe populations migrating across Europe from Ukraine brought with them a highly unequal social system and patriarchy. Our results suggest a much more dynamic picture, where social differences developed gradually. Achieving status through life-actions appears to have been more important than through inheritance, at least during the first 400 years”, says Nørtoft, the study’s lead author.

During the earliest period, approximately 2900 to 2700 BCE, burial practices suggest that the newly established communities placed considerable emphasis on shared traditions. Differences in grave wealth were relatively small and largely associated with age. There was little evidence of pronounced gender inequality, and power appeared to be distributed among several paternal lineages with steppe ancestry.

Nørtoft connects this early pattern to the circumstances surrounding the migrants’ arrival in Central Europe.

“Following a few harsh years of ‘dark sun’ clouded by a devastating volcanic eruption 2,900 BCE, the earliest herder communities, settling in Bohemia around 2,900-2,700 BCE, seem to have focused mostly on building social cohesion across this new network of migrants in Central Europe. In Bohemia, they did this through shared burial rituals, and building earthen mounds, but with few grave goods,” Mikkel Nørtoft explains.

Between approximately 2700 and 2500 BCE, however, burial customs began to change. The appearance of a new paternal lineage coincided with increasingly elaborate funerals, including greater concentrations of prestigious objects and meat offerings. Exchange networks expanded, and differences between male and female burials became more pronounced.

Adult men were particularly likely to receive richly furnished graves, while younger adults became increasingly common among those buried. Despite this growing competition for status, the skeletal evidence did not show a clear corresponding increase in injuries associated with violence.

The final phase, spanning roughly 2500 to 2300 BCE, brought further changes. One paternal lineage had become dominant in the burial record, and a small number of children received unusually wealthy burials. Because children had less opportunity to accumulate status through their own accomplishments, these graves raise the possibility that some families had begun passing social advantages between generations.

“In the final phase, roughly 2,500-2,300 BCE, we see a few rich displays of family wealth through children, and the previously new lineage now dominated the burial record. So maybe the new lineage had gained the most followers and power through the competitive burial parties, and their descendants were now competing among themselves,” Mikkel Nørtoft points out and adds:

“The few rich child graves and this prevailing lineage could indicate more inherited wealth and emerging traits of persistent inequality. Ethnographic parallels could also support the idea that parents adorned their children with ornaments to increase their social value in future marriage exchange. Brides often moved into the husband’s household in Corded Ware societies, and bridewealth or dowry is preserved in early Indo-European vocabulary, and historically common in Indo-European societies.”

The extraordinarily rich grave of a young girl at Čachovice offers a particularly striking example of this possible shift. It was the wealthiest burial among all 296 graves examined and contained an extremely rare copper neck ring. Similar neck ornaments, known as torcs, became widespread symbols of upper-class status during the later European Bronze and Iron Ages. The researchers suggest that objects placed in children’s graves may sometimes have reflected family standing or efforts to enhance their social value in future marriage arrangements, although these interpretations remain uncertain.

Taken together, the changing burial patterns suggest that competition for prestige may have gradually created more lasting social divisions within Corded Ware communities. The possibility that wealth and status were becoming hereditary is especially significant because later Bronze Age societies provide evidence of enduring family dynasties. Whether the developments in Bohemia represented early steps toward those systems remains an open question.

Researchers will need additional archaeological and genetic evidence from both the Corded Ware culture and the related Bell Beaker culture, which subsequently replaced it in Central Europe, to determine how closely burial wealth corresponded to inherited family status. The study demonstrates how archaeological evidence, ancient DNA, and linguistic history can be combined to investigate social changes that written records cannot document.

“We now have a correlation between changing Y-haplogroup lineages and unequal burial wealth display in one region, but we need more DNA data to confirm this at the family level, and elsewhere,” explains Nørtoft.

Reference: “Cooperation and Competition: Changes in Wealth, Power, and Patrilines in the Czech Corded Ware Culture” by Mikkel Nørtoft and Adam B. Rohrlach, November 2026, Journal of Neolithic Archaeology. DOI: 10.12766/jna.2026.7

#6529. Are Uranus and Neptune Secretly "Rock Giants"? A Noble Gas Might Hold the Answer

For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps. Jupiter and Saturn were the âgas giantsâ made up primarily of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune were the âice giantsâ, and were much smaller but were packed with heavier elements. A new paper from Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute and his co-authors, available in The Planetary Science Journal, explores whether we can use an isotope of a noble gas - argon-40 - to determine whether there are hidden mountains of rock under the ice giantâs thick atmospheres.

Scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock. But we canât simply fly a probe out a few billion miles and drill down into their surfaces to determine that for ourselves. Instead, they decided to use proxies, such as the concentration of argon-40, as a rough measurement for how much rock there is below the atmosphere.

Understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas. Or at least, it gives me an excuse to talk about bananas in a planetary science article. Bananas are radioactive, and the thing causing their radioactivity is potassium-40 - a relatively unstable form of a very common element. When potassium-40 decays, it turns into argon-40, which, as a noble gas, hardly interacts with anything.

Fraser talks about how to plan a mission to Uranus.

Most of this radioactive decay takes place in rocks containing potassium-40, rather than bananas, so one of the most common sources of argon-40 is literally rocks. After it is created, it bubbles up out of those rocks and escapes into its host planetâs atmosphere. In fact, it makes up around 1% of the air youâre breathing right now.

On the ice giants, this same process could hold - argon-40 could form inside a rocky surface, and then bubble up into the planetâs atmosphere over billions of years. So we should be able to send a probe to measure the concentration of argon-40 in their atmospheres, and that would serve as an effective proxy for the existence of rock under the atmosphere.

Thereâs just one catch - rocks arenât really the only source of argon-40. In fact, there was already plenty of it floating around in the protosolar nebula that the Sun and all the planets eventually formed out of. Therefore, Uranus and Neptune could have âtrappedâ this leftover argon-40 before they were even mature, causing argon-40 to eventually appear in their atmosphere, but not from rocky surfaces.

Fraser talks about efforts to go back to visit the ice giants of the solar system.

According to the paper, the amount of argon collected by the early versions of Neptune and Uranus depends entirely on where they formed with regards to the âargon ice lineâ. This line, which happens around 23-35 Kelvin, the temperature that argon freezes into solid ice, or is trapped inside water ice, is the determining factor of how much primordial argon Neptune and Uranus had sucked up.

Unfortunately, thereâs still a lot of debate about where exactly in the solar system the ice giants formed. If they formed close to the Sun and eventually migrated back out to the edges of the solar system, they might not have captured much argon ice, and the majority of the argon in their atmospheres would be due to release from rocks. On the other hand, if the theories about them actively moving through the solar system soon after their creation are true, then they would likely have captured a large amount of argon-40, making it useless as an indicator of whether or not the planets have a rocky surface.

Luckily, there is a way to potentially solve this puzzle. Argon-40 has a lighter isotopic cousin, known as argon-36, which is non-radioactive, and doesnât form in decaying rocks. Measuring its level would act like a control group, allowing scientists to estimate how much of the argon present in the atmosphere would have been swallowed at birth, as we have other estimates of the ratio between argon-40 and argon-36 in the early solar system.

Itâs good these sorts of insights are coming out now, as there is currently a mission, Uranus Orbiter and Probe, which is in active development and planned to arrive in the system in the 2040s. That still gives us some time to finalize our theories about what we would expect to find there. And perhaps, once it does arrive, weâll be able to definitively answer whether or not the âIce giantsâ have a truly solid surface or not.

After nine days in space, the Artemis II crewmembers faced their final and riskiest challenge: splashdown. In this excerpt from the book "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space," astronaut Jeremy Hansen describes the moment from his chair.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After nine days in space, the four crewmembers of NASA's Artemis II mission looked out their capsule window on April 10, 2026, and saw the bright-blue Earth below them. The crew had traveled more than 250,000 miles (400,000 kilometers) from our planet — farther from Earth than any humans had ever gone — and now, home was just a few hundred miles straight down.

Only one milestone remained: splashdown, a fast and fiery plunge into the Pacific Ocean that would mark the end of humanity's first crewed mission to the moon in more than 50 years.Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen, the lone Canadian Space Agency astronaut on the crew, had every reason to be confident that the team's Orion crew capsule would hold up just fine. But this was Hansen's first time in space, and his first time dropping through the sky like a fireball at 24,600 mph (39,600 kmh).

It wasn't that he was afraid for himself, Hansen explains in "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space" (Hanover Square Press, 2026), which he co-wrote with John Larsen). Rather, he knew that his wife Catherine and three children would be among the millions of Earthlings watching the most dangerous moment of his mission from below.

In this excerpt from the book, Hansen describes the thrilling intensity of splashdown and the euphoria of knowing that he and his crewmates were going to make it back safely — and make history.

CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen smiles inside the Orion crew capsule during the Artemis II lunar flyby.

Immediately after jettisoning the European Service Module, and exactly half an hour before we were due to splashdown, Mission Control initiated the crew module raise burn. This nineteen-second burn was the first and only burn using the small thrusters built into our Orion capsule. It slightly shallowed our entry trajectory to put us right in the sweet spot while also providing some added distance from the service module, as we'd be hitting the atmosphere in near succession. It, too, went flawlessly. I tightened my straps; it was time for the fireworks.

A re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere is absolutely on the short list of the most incredible experiences of my life. We slammed into it at 7:53 p.m., thundering down at over 10 kilometres [6.2 miles] per second. Per second.

The thrusters fired almost constantly to stabilize the capsule: loud thuds, as if Thor himself were hammering on our spacecraft, as the G-forces quickly began to build, aggressively scrubbing off the velocity we had added to our rocket nine days earlier. Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us. It started red and transformed into a bright, bluish-green, pulsating light. It was breathtaking, the bright colors igniting our senses.

It was insane to think about what we were doing. We all knew how this worked; we all knew the science. But deep inside, I also recognized that astronauts must have a screw loose to do this. Nobody in their right mind would strap themselves inside a metal canister that itself was sitting inside a giant fireball. But there was no other way down, and I had accepted the realities of this journey long in advance.

Although I was at peace, I felt guilty for the stress I was putting on my family. I had talked to them openly about the mission's risks, and this was the highest-risk moment. I tried to send my love telepathically, telling them it was going great.

The Orion capsule drops toward the Pacific Ocean with all parachutes successfully deployed.

As we continued our freefall, it looked like a thousand camera flashes were exploding inside Integrity. I lowered the sun visor on my helmet. There were only centimeters of heatshield and aluminum separating me from the more than 2500°C heat outside. Almost instantly, the heat inside our cramped home also began to rise, an increase that engineers refer to as "thermally benign." All I know is that I couldn't feel it, blissfully wrapped in my thermally controlled garments.

As we continued to fall, the G-forces built up to nearly four times the pressure we feel on Earth. I wasn't too worried, having endured more than five minutes of the same G-force, or more, in the NASA centrifuge trainer. I had half-expected the freefall back to Earth to seem short, but it was a long six minutes before the flames finally ceased and we re-established communications with Mission Control.

It had already been a wild ride, but I also knew another crazy part — parachute deployment and the actual splashdown — lay ahead. My adrenalin kept pumping.

Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us.

"Integrity, Houston. Comms check, post-blackout," we heard from Mission Control. It was music to our ears. It was exactly 8:00 p.m.

"Houston, Integrity," Reid [Wiseman, mission commander], replied. "We have you loud and clear."

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried. For the folks at NASA, it was clear that all had gone well during the descent — a small fleet of NASA and Air Force planes had captured it on high-resolution cameras. But, for me, it wasn't over yet. I wouldn't truly feel safe until our three main parachutes successfully deployed. If they didn't, we'd be a chunk of metal slamming into the ocean at incredibly high speed, and the chances of surviving that would be somewhere between minimal and non-existent.

I've watched many of my close friends return from space, and I find the minutes after surviving the re-entry heat until the parachutes deploy to be the hardest part to watch. When I see a capsule plunge through the clouds with no chutes, I always worry they might not appear at all. That's completely terrifying.

Jeremy Hansen arrives on the deck of the USS John P. Murtha after being recovered from the Orion capsule. All four crewmembers were in perfect health after splashdown.

I thought of Catherine and the kids, sending them a "don't worry, gang" message in my mind. Catherine later told me that she had a very bad feeling about the heatshield, so when we emerged from blackout, she began crying and didn't even focus on the parachutes.

Three minutes later, at an altitude of 7,100 metres, timed explosions released small chutes that pulled off the cover for two larger chutes, called drogues because they are intended to slow our acceleration to a speed that would allow our main parachutes to open without ripping. They did their job perfectly, but it was wild inside the capsule, jerking us back and forth like a ride at the fair.

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried.

One minute later, at only 1,500 metres above the ocean, the drogue chutes cut loose, and, for a few moments, we felt like we were falling backward. Then, in succession, the three main parachutes began deploying, blossoming slowly so they wouldn't tear apart. The rate of our fall slowed as the red-and-white nylon canopies, each 35 metres in diameter, filled with air. The thrusters kept firing, aiming the capsule's base directly toward the point of impact.

"Integrity, we see three good-looking parachutes," we heard from our CAPCOM. Within seconds, our splashdown speed had reduced to 27 kilometres per hour.

That's it, I said to myself. I'm pretty sure we can survive whatever else could be thrown at us now.

Christina [Koch, mission specialist] seemed to agree. We grabbed one another's hands in a moment of celebration.

Excerpted from "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, The Groundbreaking Human Mission Into Deep Space" by John Larsen with Jeremy Hansen. © 2026 by John Larsen, used with permission by HarperCollins/Hanover Square Press.

#6527. Heart Stents May Not Prevent Heart Attacks or Early Death, Landmark Study Finds

A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.

For someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step. Yet improving blood flow and preventing future health problems are separate goals, and a procedure that achieves one may not necessarily achieve the other.

Researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial. They found no statistically significant difference in the combined risk of death or heart attack between patients initially assigned to an artery-opening procedure plus medical therapy and those assigned to medical therapy alone.

Published in JAMA and presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, the findings offer an unusually long look at how these treatment strategies compare.

The original COURAGE trial enrolled people with stable coronary artery disease and compared optimal medical therapy alone with optimal medical therapy plus percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), commonly known as angioplasty.

During angioplasty, doctors inflate a small balloon inside a narrowed artery to improve blood flow. They often place a tiny metal tube called a stent to help keep the artery open.

For the new analysis, researchers tracked 959 participants through linked health records. The median follow-up was 15 years, with some patients followed for as long as 25 years. The estimated 25-year cumulative incidence of death or heart attack was 93.3% in the group initially assigned to PCI plus medical therapy and 91% in the medical therapy group. That difference was not statistically significant.

Earlier research had examined long-term survival after the trial. This analysis also included heart attacks, allowing researchers to assess whether an initial PCI strategy might prevent cardiovascular events that would not be captured by survival figures alone.

The central finding concerns what happens after an artery has been successfully opened. Restoring blood flow can relieve symptoms, but the study did not find evidence that starting with PCI lowered the combined long-term risk of heart attack or death.

“When we open a blocked artery, we know we’ve improved blood flow through that artery, and that relieves symptoms. But the bigger question is whether that translates into a reduction in clinical events such as heart attacks or death for patients over the long term. That’s what we wanted to understand with this study,” said Butala, an assistant professor of medicine-cardiology at the CU Anschutz School of Medicine.

“We found no significant difference in the risk of death or heart attack between the two treatment groups. That’s important information for doctors and patients as they consider the best approach to treating stable coronary artery disease.”

These results do not mean angioplasty and stents are unnecessary. They can relieve chest pain and other symptoms, while emergency procedures can be lifesaving during certain types of heart attacks. The study specifically examined an initial PCI strategy for stable coronary disease, so its findings should be understood within that setting.

Although the participants came from a randomized trial, this analysis was a post hoc observational follow-up, rather than a new randomized trial. It included veterans whose health records could be linked, a group with higher baseline health risks than the full COURAGE trial population.

The researchers also acknowledged limitations in identifying heart attacks through routinely collected health records. However, the findings were consistent with events independently verified during the original trial.

The research helps clarify what an initial procedure may accomplish. Symptom relief remains a meaningful benefit, but the long-term findings do not establish additional protection against heart attack or death compared with medical therapy alone. Butala said considering both immediate relief and future health outcomes can support more informed treatment decisions.

Reference: “Percutaneous Coronary Intervention and Long-Term Outcomes in Stable Coronary Artery Disease: Extended Follow-Up of the COURAGE Randomized Trial” by Neel M. Butala, Nandini Murali, Natalia Rahman, Shayna Cave, Siamack Ayandeh, Mary E. Plomondon, Jonathan W. Cunningham, William S. Weintraub, Robert W. Yeh, Stephen W. Waldo and William E. Boden, 7 November 2026, JAMA. DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.23488

#6526. The Simons Observatory is Online and Surveying the Cosmic Microwave Background

The Simons Observatory in the Atacama Desert has begun its mission to survey the Cosmic Microwave Background. Its goal is to detect undeniable evidence of the Big Bang and cosmic inflation. Can this unique survey succeed where others have failed?

We live in an age of large astronomical surveys, enabled by powerful computers and data handling methods. While powerful telescopes still perform detailed observations of individual targets, and always will, wide surveys have a power all their own. The ESA's Gaia mission, for example, has completed its survey of billions of stars and generated a massive amount of foundational data that researchers will draw on for decades to come.

There are automated surveys for transients like supernovae and asteroids, radio-sky surveys to spot objects obscured by thick dust, and massive surveys just getting started like the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's three core surveys.

But another Simons Observatory's survey hasn't garnered the same attention that some of the other have. The Simons Observatory (SO) consists of four telescopes working together: three small 0.5 meter aperture 'scopes in its Small Aperture Telescope (SAT) and one large 6-meter one in its Large Aperture Telescope (LAT).

The unusual configuration gives the SO the best chance to observe tiny details in the Universe's first observable light, the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB).

This image of the Cosmic Microwave Background is from the Simons Observatory, the newest and most powerful observatory to study the CMB. It's unique arrangement of three small and one large telescope increases its resolution by an order of magnitude over its predecessor, the Planck satellite. The Simons Observatory's main goal is to find the elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation, and thereby confirming the Big Bang model of cosmology. Image Credit: Simons Observatory.

The stuff of the Universe was too opaque for light to travel through it at first. Photons were effectively scattered by the hot, dense plasma that permeated the Universe. Eventually conditions changed. The Universe expanded, the plasma cooled, and photons could travel. This was the recombination epoch and it occurred about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

Note that the name is historical and reflected our earlier understanding of the Universe. It wasn't actually a recombination, it was the first time that electrons and protons combined to form neutral hydrogen, and that's what made the cosmos transparent. Its name should probably be changed to the combination epoch.

But regardless of its name, the cosmic microwave background is the relic radiation from the Universe's first light, and it holds clues to the Universe, especially to the Big Bang theory of cosmology.

Other efforts have been made to map the CMB. NASA's Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) and the ESA's Planck satellite both made the effort from orbit. Currently, the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and related facilities are doing the same.

The SPT made an important discovery. It detected for the first time what's called the B-mode polarization of the CMB. The B-mode is important because it was created by primordial gravitational waves generated during the epoch of inflation, the first moments of the Universe's inflation. So finding the B-mode was important evidence for the Big Bang theory.

The South Pole Telescope at the AmundsenâScott South Pole Station, Antarctica. The SPT is a 10-meter telescope that is credited with the first detection of the Cosmic Microwave Background's B-mode polarization. Image Credit: By Amble - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/9057466

But there was a problem. Gravitational lensing can also create B-mode polarization, and it has nothing to do with the Big Bang or inflation. It's difficult to tell which source created the B-mode polarization the SPT detected. So its initial detection was put in doubt.

This is where the Simons Observatory comes into the picture. It's been calibrating its instruments for two years and is now getting down to business.

âTo have all the observatory motors humming, gears turning and data flowing makes me joyful, but even more exciting is the prospect of what we could find in its big new deep and detailed maps,â says Simons Observatory Co-Director Suzanne Staggs of Princeton University.

This time-lapse shows the Simons Observatory's Large Area Telescope scanning the sky in August 2026. Credit: David Boettger

The observatory's four telescopes collectively have tens of thousands of microwave detectors, almost 98,000 of them. That's 16 times more than one of its predecessors, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. They're not only mapping the CMB the same way that WMAP and the Planck satellite did. They're also searching for the tiny fluctuations in the CMB, the B-mode polarizations that can confirm the Big Bang and cosmic inflation. If detected, the SO can determine if these are true artifacts of primordial gravitational waves, or artifacts of the polluting gravitational lensing that confounded the SPT.

It'll take years of observations before that can be achieved, but the SO's first observations are already showing the observatory's power. Its sensitivity is meant to be an order of magnitude highter than its predecessor, the Planck satellite. âThe images that weâve made with just a few months of data are already deeper and less noisy than Planckâs, which were collected over years,â says Simons Observatory Spokesperson Jo Dunkley of Princeton University. That's significant, because the Planck outperformed its predecessor, WMAP, and is considered the benchmark for CMB observations. So the SO is already establishing a new benchmark for observations.

The SO's unique four telescope design is already showing its value. The large, 6-meter telescope is able to observe more of the sky in higher resolution than other CMB telescopes. Every couple of days, it scans half of the available sky.

âIt is incredibly satisfying to see the early maps, knowing that our initial data places us at the forefront of the field â and that we are poised to go much further,â says Jeffrey McMahon, observatory testing lead at the University of Chicago.

The SO isn't isolated and alone in its work. All of these CMB surveys and observatories will work together in the end. For example, the SPT and other facilities at its site are mapping gravitational lenses that can interfere with the detection of B-modes from primordial gravitational waves in the epoch of inflation. Those templates can be used to help remove their pollution from CMB surveys. So it's all hands on deck.

This cut-away schematic shows the Large Area Telescope's Receiver with one of its optical tubes highlighted. Note the pulse tube coolers and the dilution refrigerator. They keep the telescope at the cryogenic temperatures necessary for microwave observations. Image Credit: Simons Observatory/Nicholas Galitzki et al. 2018. Conference Proceedings.

The SO is an observer of polarized light, and that means that while its primary goal is searching for B-mode polarization, its maps have other things to reveal, too. âThere are a number of large surveys adding to our understanding of the universe,â Staggs says. âOur idea is that we can combine our data with theirs to further our discoveries.â

This is especially true of other wide surveys like the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time. The pair will create a potent combination for detecting transients across multiple wavelengths. âThe instrument is now sensitive enough that we can see small changes in transients in only a few days, whereas ACT took months,â Devlin says. âThis enables us to observe entirely new classes of objects.â Its science observations have barely begun, and it's already giant stellar flares and asteroids in the Milky Way, and activity around a supermassive black holes outside of our galaxy.

But detecting that elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation is the SO's holy grail, and if it finds it, it will be a collective finding in the mass data the observatory will produce. Like other survey telescopes, the data will be released in large sequential data releases.

âWeâll be providing everything to the community through a data management tool, which we hope to have completed for the first data release,â Devlin says.

The initial success of its first science operations is a hopeful indication that it can finally find the evidence of cosmic inflation, the B-mode polarization from primordial gravitational waves in the CMB.

âEssentially, right out of the box, just turning on the instrument, weâre making beautiful crisp images of the Milky Way,â Staggs says. Those images are uncovering new observations of the galaxy's magnetic fields, and understanding them is critical to understanding star formation and how the galaxy evolves.

âThis moment marks a major milestone in our effort to understand these big questions about the universe,â Devlin says. âI think thereâs going to be so many scientific discoveries coming out in the next few years, itâll be hard to keep up.â

The SO's performance will improve when another three small telescopes are added in 2027. That will also double the Small Area Telescope's number of individual detectors to 48,160 detectors. The original five-year survey has been extended, too.

"Combined with a planned extension of the survey duration to 2035, this expansion will significantly enhance SO's search for a B-mode signal in the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background, a potential signature of gravitational waves produced in the very early Universe," explain the authors of a 2026 paper in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

The holiday gift season is not far off. For me, I’d rather spend December enjoying myself than panic-shopping for someone who claims they “don’t need anything.” Especially when that same person has been borrowing my tools all year long. If you’ve got a DIYer, weekend tinkerer, or devoted Milwaukee fan on your gift list, now’s a good time to get some shopping out of the way—and you don’t need a several-hundred-dollar power tool to make their day.

As a tool guy myself, I’d much rather unwrap something useful than another novelty gift destined for the attic. Give me a compact drill/driver that makes a repair easier, a utility knife that replaces the battered one in my pocket, or a magnetic tape measure that saves me from constantly asking, “Hey, can you hold this?” Shopping for someone who practically lives under a car? A cordless power ratchet might be just the thing to loosen those stubborn fittings. And if we’re talking about a holiday gift exchange, who doesn’t want to bring the present everyone wants to steal?

With all of that in mind, we’ve rounded up these Milwaukee gifts for less than $100. Whether you’re shopping for a loved one building their first tool kit or someone who’s garage is already bathed in the glow of red tools and white lightning bolts, there’s something here well worth the time and energy it takes to wrap it.

Milwaukee Shockwave Impact Driver Bit Set (74-Piece Set)

Few things are more annoying than hunting through your tool kit for the proper-sized drive bit. This 74-piece set keeps all of your bits in one handy kit that makes them easy to reach and simple to remove. This kit really covers the fastening basics, as it includes various sizes of star bits, Phillips-head bits, and an assortment of standard slot-head sizes. I particularly like that Milwaukee included 1/4- and 5/16-inch hex drive bits—two I’m usually rooting around for—in the sturdy kit.

Milwaukee Fastback Folding Utility Knife with Multifunctionality

This sharp, serrated knife lives in that space between a razor, a utility knife, and a bare-bones multi-tool. The housing is sturdy and well-built, and the knife itself holds an edge for an exceptionally long time. Serrations are perfect for cutting heavy rope, which might come in handy for the camper or boat enthusiast in your life. And the swing-out screwdriver is more than just a gimmick in that it’s strong enough to handle prying with the slot head in place or extracting a stubborn Phillips head with that drive head locked in. And in the end, you can crack a beer with the built-in opener.

Milwaukee 12V Cordless 1/2-Inch Hammer Drill/Driver

For the Milwaukee fan who already has M12 batteries on hand, this compact hammer drill is a gift that’ll get put to work over and over. Its brushless motor handles everyday drilling and driving, and the hammer setting adds the ability to drill holes in brick and masonry with the right bit. The chuck accommodates bits up to 1/2-inch in diameter, but its all-metal construction grips smaller bits, drivers, and nut runners with equal strength. Many contractors—electricians among them—favor its compact size, which makes the drill easier to maneuver in tight spaces or between studs. I’ve long been a fan of Milwaukee’s more compact M12 oscillating tool. For one, it’s easy to use in tight spaces due to its size. More importantly, it’s a powerhouse. I’m partial to tools I can keep handy as I work on projects, especially if I'm in a tight spot like an attic or crawl space. I want a multi-tool that isn’t too bulky. This oscillating tool is perfect for cutting notches or pockets in lumber or trimming door jamb bases to better slip tile or wood flooring under. Milwaukee Set of 12 Tri-Lobe Screwdrivers

Milwaukee Class A Type 3 Packout First Aid Kit (79-Piece) with 100 Lumens Pen Light

#6524. The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever new ideas have been simmering since last year’s big meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director

I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman

Tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest

This is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated quickly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be said is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

#6523. Alzheimer’s Breakthrough: Researchers Find New Clues to Cognitive Decline in Healthy Adults

Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.

A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years. In a new Mayo Clinic study published in JAMA Neurology, researchers developed a method that combines an Alzheimer’s-related blood biomarker with age, sex, and genetic risk to produce personalized estimates.

For example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low. At a higher level, that estimate rose to 16%. Her predicted 10-year risk increased from 12% to 35%.

The method measures phosphorylated Tau 217 (p-tau217), a protein associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Elevated levels in the blood are linked to Alzheimer’s-related changes in the brain, but a positive biomarker result alone cannot determine whether or when someone will develop cognitive symptoms.

“The goal is to provide a personalized estimate of the risk of developing cognitive impairment that is more meaningful than simply reporting whether a blood test is positive or negative for amyloid pathology,” says Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic laboratory medicine and pathology researcher and first author of the study.

The research builds on an earlier Mayo Clinic prediction model that used positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans to detect amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease. Measuring p-tau217 in blood offers a less invasive approach that could be used more widely.

Researchers analyzed data from 1,644 cognitively healthy participants in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and 534 participants in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. All were between 60 and 90 years old and had undergone blood biomarker measurements, genetic testing, and repeated cognitive assessments.

Using the Mayo Clinic data, the team calculated the probability of developing MCI or dementia within five or 10 years. Higher p-tau217 levels and older age were associated with greater risk. At the same elevated biomarker level, the estimated five-year risk of MCI was 6% for a 65-year-old but 37% for an 85-year-old.

The researchers then examined the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data, which independently supported the association between elevated p-tau217 and increased risk of cognitive decline.

The approach could eventually help doctors identify people who might benefit from preventive treatment before memory problems begin. However, its clinical usefulness will depend partly on whether therapies can successfully delay cognitive decline in people who have no symptoms.

“A person may want to know: What is my risk of developing cognitive impairment in the next five or 10 years, and how does this blood test change that risk?” says Ronald Petersen, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and director of the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging. “If preventive therapies prove effective, those numbers could become very important in treatment decisions.”

Clinical trials, including AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3, are investigating whether treatments targeting amyloid can delay cognitive decline before symptoms develop. Both trials have used blood biomarkers to help identify participants, highlighting their potential role in earlier Alzheimer’s research.

“Absolute risk gives the biomarker result clinical context,” says Clifford Jack Jr., M.D., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist and senior author of the study. “If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about the potential benefits and risks of treatment.”

The risk estimates were developed using the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and require further evaluation in more diverse populations and with other p-tau217 blood tests. Although the findings support the potential of personalized risk prediction, Alzheimer’s biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without cognitive symptoms.

Reference: “Absolute Risk of Progression to Cognitive Impairment Based on Plasma Phosphorylated Tau 217, Age, Sex, and APOE ε4” by Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Mingzhao Hu, Stephen D. Weigand, et al., 16 November 2026, JAMA Neurology. DOI: 10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.4292
