#6512. NASA Smashed Into an Asteroid. Now ESA’s Hera Spacecraft Is About to Reveal the Damage

The European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has reached the two asteroids it was sent to investigate, marking a major milestone in a mission designed to strengthen Earth’s defenses against dangerous space rocks. Roughly the size of a small car, Hera is now traveling just 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system, which consists of a larger asteroid and its smaller companion, Dimorphos.

The spacecraft has entered its initial observation period, known as the ‘early characterization phase’. During this stage, researchers are collecting essential information about both asteroids, with particular attention to Dimorphos, which NASA deliberately struck with a spacecraft in 2022 to test whether an asteroid’s path could be changed.

“Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission’s planetary defense goals,” explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

“During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022.

“Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one – if any!”

Navigating around two small asteroids presents challenges unlike those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The biggest difference is gravity, which is extraordinarily weak around these small bodies.

Didymos, the larger asteroid, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravity roughly 40,000 times weaker than Earth’s. Its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, is about 151 meters wide, with gravity approximately 200,000 times weaker than Earth’s.

These conditions make a conventional circular orbit impractical. Instead, Hera moves around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second, comparable to a fast crawling insect.

Rather than continuously curving around its targets, Hera follows a series of nearly straight paths. During a repeating sequence of three days followed by four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers produce a series of rectangular flight patterns that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

The technique builds on lessons from ESA’s Rosetta comet mission. Its biggest advantage is safety. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther into space instead of heading toward a potentially damaging collision. The slow flight speed also means that each course correction requires very little fuel.

Hera’s current observations are only the beginning. Next month, the mission is expected to enter its ‘detailed characterization phase’, bringing the spacecraft closer to the asteroids for more thorough measurements.

During this stage, Hera will begin following more complicated trajectories shaped like bowties. These paths, made up of hyperbolic arcs, will initially take the spacecraft to distances of approximately 20 kilometers from its targets.

The mission is directed from ESA’s ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Controllers communicate with Hera for approximately eight hours each day, despite the spacecraft being about 196.5 million kilometers away.

Those communications travel through four massive Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

Supporting the controllers is ESA’s Flight Dynamics team. Specialists analyze information transmitted by Hera to pinpoint its location relative to the asteroids. They then calculate the commands needed to guide the spacecraft safely to its next position.

Hera’s primary scientific target is Dimorphos, which became the focus of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment on September 26, 2022.

That day, NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at 6.1 kilometers per second, sending a vast cloud of debris spreading across approximately 10,000 kilometers of space.

The experiment achieved its main objective. The collision shortened Dimorphos’ orbital period around Didymos by approximately 33 minutes, demonstrating that a spacecraft could alter an asteroid’s motion through a direct impact.

However, the results also raised important questions. The change in Dimorphos’ orbit was significantly greater than scientists had predicted, suggesting that the asteroid responded to the collision in ways that existing models did not fully capture.

Researchers still do not know exactly how much physical damage the collision caused. Did DART create a large crater, or did the force of the impact substantially reshape Dimorphos? Scientists also need more precise measurements of the asteroid’s mass, composition, and internal structure to understand why the deflection was so effective.

Answering these questions is essential before the technique, known as ‘kinetic impact’, can become a dependable option for protecting Earth from a potentially hazardous asteroid.

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed ‘crash site investigation’ of Dimorphos, using its scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and the aftermath of the DART collision.

The spacecraft will also release two shoebox-sized ‘CubeSats’. These miniature spacecraft will approach the asteroids even more closely, gathering additional observations before the mission eventually progresses to landing operations.

Together, the measurements could reveal how Dimorphos absorbed and responded to the impact, helping scientists determine which predictions were accurate and why the asteroid’s orbit changed more than expected.

By turning NASA’s successful experiment into a better-understood planetary defense method, Hera could play an important role in preparing humanity to deflect an asteroid that might otherwise threaten Earth.

#6510. ESA's Hera Probe Uses "Superhuman" Vision to Inspect NASA's Asteroid Crash Site

Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

The lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

To help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

In the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

However, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

But why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

Crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

But ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

#6509. Amazon’s New 6-Inch Kindle Is So Small, I Bring Mine Everywhere

This tiny e-reader is fast, cute, and built for commuting.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Amazon just gave its Kindle lineup a major makeover, and the smallest model might be the most exciting. Earlier this month, the company introduced a redesigned 6-inch Kindle that's more compact than any e-reader users have seen before. It’s got a sleek new look, faster performance, and four gorgeous colors that make the popular device feel like a cute accessory in its own right. After spending some time with the new Alpine Sky version, I can confidently say that its tiny size is one of my favorite things about it.

The new Kindle is officially Amazon's most pocket-sized e-reader yet, featuring a redesigned flush-front display that eliminates the raised border around the screen. The 6-inch, 300-ppi glare-free display is still black and white, but the device itself now has color that stretches seamlessly from front to back. Amazon also says the new Kindle opens books 30 percent faster than its predecessor and offers up to six weeks of battery life on a single charge, which has been ideal for me, someone who forgets to charge any of his devices.

One of the biggest updates is the introduction of two different versions of the 6-inch Kindle. The standard model starts at $149.99 and comes in Ube (a pretty purple shade) and classic Graphite, with 16 GB of storage. For $189.99, you can upgrade to the new Kindle Aluminum, which comes in Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green, with a premium matte aluminum back, 32GB of storage, and no lock-screen ads.

I have the Alpine Sky version, which has a beautiful, soft blue finish that always gets compliments from friends. But beyond the new colors and materials, I've appreciated most how easy this little thing is to bring everywhere. I live in New York City, so I'm constantly taking the subway, and carrying a physical book around isn't always convenient. It’s not impossible, but it can be a nuisance when I'm reading something particularly thick. The Kindle is smaller than most of the books I own, takes up little room in my bag, and feels comfortable to hold for longer reading sessions without making my hand ache.

I also love that I can throw it into pretty much any bag I'm carrying, whether it's a small everyday bag or something much larger. And, admittedly, there's something funny about watching other commuters on the subway notice it. I swear I can see people clocking the tiny blue Kindle and thinking how cute it is (but that could just be my main-character energy). The text is still plenty readable despite its smaller display, and sometimes I feel like the person sitting next to me is following along with whatever chapter I'm on.

Of course, the smaller Kindle doesn't have every feature you'll find on Amazon's pricier models. It lacks waterproofing and adjustable warm lighting like the Kindle Paperwhite, so readers who prioritize those features may prefer the larger option. But if you want a convenient, portable way to read, there's plenty to appreciate here.

The new 6-inch Kindle and Kindle Aluminum are available to shop now, with prices starting at $149.99. Whether you're new to e-reading or just want something smaller for your commute, Amazon's latest release makes a pretty convincing case for carrying an entire library in your bag.

#6508. An Overlooked Property of Light Could Open the Door to a New Era of Optical Computing

Monitoring electricity in buried cables could one day become easier thanks to an overlooked magnetic effect in optical fibers, although researchers still need to overcome a major sensitivity challenge.

For decades, engineers have used optical fibers to measure magnetic fields around electrical cables, but these sensors generally need to wrap around the conductor to work. Now, researchers in South Africa have discovered that a magnetic field can also affect light when it points sideways across a fiber, challenging an assumption that has guided optical engineering for more than 50 years.

The finding, published in Optics Letters, could eventually lead to sensors that sit alongside electrical cables rather than surrounding them. It may also offer a new way to control light for optical computing.

MSc student Mohammed Raiyan Sharif and Professor Mitchell Cox at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg demonstrated the previously overlooked interaction, known as the transverse Faraday effect. Their research was conducted at the Wits Optical Communication (OC) Lab in the university’s School of Electrical and Information Engineering.

Optical fibers carry internet signals through thin strands of glass, but they can also detect magnetic fields. This sensing ability relies on the Faraday effect, first observed by Michael Faraday in glass in 1845. When a magnetic field points along the direction light travels, it slightly rotates the light’s polarization, or the direction in which its electric field oscillates. Measuring that rotation can reveal the strength of the magnetic field and the electrical current producing it.

A sideways magnetic field was not expected to produce the same effect. To investigate, Sharif and Cox placed strong magnets beside a stationary multimode optical fiber without touching it, then watched the light emerging from the other end.

Multimode fibers have relatively wide glass cores that allow light to travel along many different paths, repeatedly reflecting off the core’s mirror-like boundary. At the output, the overlapping waves create a pattern of bright and dark spots called speckle, similar to the shifting patterns inside a kaleidoscope.

As the researchers rearranged the magnets, a camera recorded changes in that pattern. The sideways magnetic field was somehow altering the light’s behavior inside the fiber.

“It wasn’t hard to 3D print a rig to test our intuition. Working out the theory for what we were seeing was the challenging part,” says Sharif. “The key was to return to the underlying equations and question assumptions that are usually taken for granted in fiber optics.”

The explanation involved a small part of the light wave that a widely used mathematical shortcut ignores. Known as the weak-guidance approximation, this approach assumes that light’s electric field oscillates almost entirely across the fiber, leaving out a tiny component that oscillates along its length.

The approximation works extremely well when the fiber’s core and surrounding glass have similar refractive indices, which describe how strongly a material slows light. However, Sharif and Cox tested step-index fibers, where the refractive index changes abruptly at the core’s boundary rather than gradually, as it does in graded-index fibers.

When that difference is large, the normally neglected longitudinal component becomes significant near the core’s edge. By including it in their equations, the researchers showed that a sideways magnetic field transfers some of the light’s transverse oscillation into the longitudinal component. This changes how light reflects inside the fiber and, ultimately, the speckle pattern it produces.

The team also distinguished the new interaction from the Cotton-Mouton effect, another response to sideways magnetic fields. The Cotton-Mouton effect increases with the square of the magnetic field’s strength, while the transverse Faraday effect increases in direct proportion to it.

Their measurements confirmed four predictions. The effect disappeared without a sufficiently strong step in refractive index, became stronger when light entered at steeper angles, occurred for only one polarization relative to the magnetic field, and varied with wavelength in the same way as the conventional Faraday effect.

With a magnetic field of 0.24 tesla, roughly the strength found close to a powerful neodymium magnet, light polarized across the field produced a speckle pattern only about 84% similar to the original.

“What is surprising is finding an overlooked, useful interaction in such a familiar technology,” says Cox. “It’s quite exciting that there is always something new to learn or discover, and often these things are right under our noses, hidden in the assumptions we have made for decades.”

One possible application is monitoring electrical currents with fibers laid alongside cables, including those buried in trenches. However, magnetic fields near most cables are much weaker than those used in the experiment, so the sensitivity of a practical sensor remains uncertain.

The researchers also envision replacing permanent magnets with electrical coils, allowing currents to control the patterns of light traveling through a fiber.

“Besides sensing, I think that being able to control different modes (patterns of light) inside the fiber electrically could unlock a new way to do optical computing,” says Cox. “We can model the way light gets distorted when it propagates through fibers, frosted glass windows, or even the atmosphere. If we change our perspective on those models, we can actually use light to do mathematical computations for us, for free.”

Reference: “Transverse Faraday effect in multimode fibers” by Mohammed R. Sharif and Mitchell A. Cox, 30 September 2026, Optics Letters. DOI: 10.1364/OL.611078

The research was supported by the South African Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and the National Research Foundation (NRF).

#6507. The Best Little Gifts Your Holiday Party Host Will Actually Want

Don’t show up empty-handed or with a cheap bottle of wine — bring status cocktail cherries, a beeswax candle, or a painterly placemat

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A good host is always thinking of others, whether it’s by making guests feel welcome, accommodating everyone’s diets, or setting an Instagram-worthy tablescape to make the night feel extra special. But the holiday season is an opportunity to flip the script and show the host you’re thinking of them, too. Bringing them a gift is the cardinal way to thank the host for all their thoughtful work. The only question remains: what to give?

For those who delight in trotting out their special dinnerware for guests, there’s a world of creative and whimsical gifts out there, even if it seems like they already have the entire CB2 catalog. And if that is the case, this just means you, as the gift-giver, can allow them to indulge in the things they typically would not. Take, for instance, some unique vintage shot glasses, intricately carved chopsticks, and pearl cocktail picks. Not only do these playful takes on essentials inspire joy, but they’re also sure to be conversation starters for future gatherings. And, as the bestower of the new treasured piece, you just might secure yourself the invite for the next one.

You can never have enough serving utensils if you love to host. That moment when you toss your pasta salad, plate everyone’s green beans, or dole out your main dish is an opportunity to flex some of your more decorative yet functional kitchen tools. This ethereal stainless steel set from Leif boasts pewter star-shaped handles with sea glass.

Even Diaspora Spice Co.’s everyday spices come in bold, ready-to-gift packaging, but the equitable spice company’s new holiday spice sampler gift box is an extra colorful treat for the senses. The bundle includes samples of its beloved Nandini coriander, a rare Ceylon cinnamon, a Himalayan foothills-sourced pink garlic powder, and several more spices to inspire your host.

When it comes to gift-giving, we believe in working smarter, not harder. Case in point: Buy a set of nice-looking vintage glasses — these are labeled shot glasses by the seller, but they’re just as nice for sipping cordials — and rather than giving one lovely host a set of eight, split them up into pairs or fours and use them for multiple gifting situations. There’s always a use for little glasses like this (and they’re pretty enough to display, too).

It’s pretty fun to use a posh plaid napkin when you’re digging into some quiche or sipping on mulled wine.

It’s always fun to kick off an evening of cocktails with a caviar bump, which is what makes this Imperia Caviar bundle such a gift for the avid party host. The 30-gram tin of royal ossetra comes with a mother-of-pearl spoon and a caviar tin opener in a velvet bag, and the bundle’s compact size means you can simply slide it into your purse or jacket on the way to the function (unlike a heavy bottle of wine or olive oil, which would likely need their owns bags).

It really has been the year of the dirty martini. For those who are building a bar cart (or want to start), getting a couple of sets of proper cocktail picks can be a game-changer. Nothing wrong with a traditional wood toothpick, of course, but it really does add a lot of pizzazz to a martini to bite the olives off a pearl-emblazoned skewer.

Swooning will abound once people get a look at these beautiful walnut chopsticks featuring inlaid geometric designs. Another great example of “practical, but nicer to look at than what you might get for yourself.” Plus, you can grab a set of five on sale right now for under $20.

When it comes to cocktail cherries, one brand truly reigns supreme: Luxardo, which has been making candied cherries soaked in marasca syrup for 120 years. A classic for a reason!

Jonathan Adler is another designer to keep tabs on when it comes to playful but elevated home decor. This set of Matisse-esque coasters also has a slight lip to keep condensation from spilling, and would be prime for serving up lychee martinis the next time you gather with friends. Snag them while they’re 40% off for Black Friday.

Halen Môn is a salt nerd’s dream. The organic, hand-harvested sea salt hails from the tides of the Isle of Anglesey in Wales (Halen is Welsh for salt; Môn is Welsh for Anglesey), and has earned numerous awards for its subtle crunch and crisp mineral flavor. Any host would be thrilled to receive a bag of the stuff, but this gift set combines the salt with a charming ceramic cellar and spoon.

Matches are always a solid host gift, and a small but useful present that’s made all the better with cool packaging. The lifestyle brand State the Label, for example, has housed its matches in a folk art-inspired cottage (the striker paper is on the bottom of the house).

Those who like to entertain likely appreciate a good placemat. This set of two block-printed placemats from West Elm puts a romantic spin on the dining-table staple with painterly tones and bright hues. Who wouldn’t love to receive these dreamy accents?

Is your host a lover of ice-cold martinis? Perfect gift incoming: Quincy’s fabulous olives, which have superb flavor and are ratioed with drink-perfect brine to make exactly 14 dirty martinis per jar.

Scents are tricky. Unless you really know your host, refrain from gifting them scented candles, and opt for a beeswax pillar candle instead; they can light it sans candelabra (unless you’re sure that they own one and prefer tapers) by simply placing it on a small plate. Above all, beeswax candles make a wonderful dining companion, because they don’t emit the same stuffy, paraffin wax-based smoke as non-beeswax candles.

Sometimes, brevity is wit. Give it to someone who means business, or orders the business women special.

We all love a little Le Creuset in our kitchens, but a Dutch oven isn’t in the price range for what we’d consider an easy host gift. Enter the butter dish, a fabulous little thing to present and say “I brought you something,” presented with a kiss on the cheek and maybe a bouquet of flowers or bottle of wine.

#6506. Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a big part of understanding the present-day Earth.

Earth is one big system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a new trick with them: photosynthesis.

Cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

But this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

New research in The Innovation shows how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations."

The oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

The researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research shows that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on new geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide new constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

The researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

They found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

The second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

The researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

This graphic illustrates the results from new research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that shows how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

On shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it shows that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

Over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life."

This figure shows the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

It all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work shows that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

The pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

Understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

Recently, researchers used AI to "decode" segments of birdsong. In the wake of this, Live Science asks its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The idea of talking to animals like Dr. Dolittle might sound far-fetched, but researchers are making progress toward understanding how other species communicate. In a recent Live Science interview, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie explained how she used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the calls of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata). For instance, Elie was able to determine which calls the birds used to communicate over short distances versus longer distances.

Birds aren't the only animals scientists are hoping to understand. Researchers with Project CETI are using AI to decipher the clicks and calls of sperm whales, while a separate team (with the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI) conducted what they described as the first "conversation" between humans and a humpback whale. The whale, named Twain, responded to recorded calls played by researchers over a 20 minute period, a "conversation" scientists believe could help us figure out how to communicate with extraterrestrial life someday.

Closer to home, cats have already figured out how to use meows to get their human's attention, whether they're demanding food, affection or simply that we open the door for them (again). Whether this means they understand the human language or not is still up for debate, but it raises an interesting question: If we could understand what animals were saying, which species would you most want to talk to? Vote in our poll and let us know what you'd ask in the comments below!

#6504. New Once-Daily Pill Slashes Bad Cholesterol by Nearly 65% in Clinical Trial

A pill taken before breakfast cut “bad” cholesterol by nearly two-thirds in a trial of people already taking statins.

High cholesterol can silently damage blood vessels for decades, increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes without causing noticeable symptoms. Much of that danger comes from excess LDL (“bad”) cholesterol, which contributes to fatty plaque buildup inside artery walls. Although statins help millions of people control their cholesterol, some patients need additional treatment to bring their levels down.

A newly approved once-daily pill could provide another option. Lipfendra (enlicitide) reduced LDL cholesterol by nearly 65% in a clinical trial involving adults already taking statins. Approved by the FDA on July 16, 2026, it is the first oral medication in a powerful class of cholesterol treatments previously available only through injections.

Enlicitide targets PCSK9, a protein that influences how efficiently the liver removes LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream. Normally, PCSK9 promotes the destruction of LDL receptors on liver cells. When these receptors are lost, the liver becomes less effective at clearing circulating cholesterol.

By blocking PCSK9, enlicitide allows more LDL receptors to remain active, helping the liver remove additional cholesterol from the blood. Unlike earlier PCSK9 inhibitors that require injections, enlicitide uses a specialized macrocyclic peptide formulation with absorption-enhancing ingredients, allowing the medication to be taken orally.

A review published in Annals of Pharmacotherapy found that enlicitide reduced LDL cholesterol by 57.1% to 64.6% after 24 weeks across clinical trials. These reductions were comparable to those achieved with injectable PCSK9 inhibitors.

In a direct comparison involving patients already taking statins, LDL cholesterol fell by approximately 65% with enlicitide. By comparison, reductions were about 28% with ezetimibe and 6% with bempedoic acid, two other oral medications used to manage high cholesterol.

The review examined research identified through PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane through July 17, 2026. Participants included adults with elevated cholesterol and those with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, an inherited condition that causes unusually high LDL cholesterol levels from birth and increases the risk of premature cardiovascular disease.

In the largest trial, adverse effects occurred at similar rates among participants receiving enlicitide and those taking a placebo. However, a separate study involving people with inherited high cholesterol reported more diarrhea and dizziness among those receiving the medication. Longer-term monitoring will help establish its safety with continued use.

Enlicitide must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach. Patients may drink water, black coffee, or plain tea with the medication but must wait at least 30 minutes before consuming food or other beverages. A 30-day supply carries a list price of $315, although actual costs depend on insurance coverage.

While clinical trials have established that enlicitide substantially reduces LDL cholesterol, researchers have not yet determined whether it also prevents heart attacks and strokes. An ongoing cardiovascular outcomes trial is investigating whether its cholesterol-lowering effects translate into fewer serious cardiovascular events.

Reference: “Enlicitide: The First Oral PCSK9i for Lowering Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol” by Rachel C. Lucas, Mia E. Lussier, Azadeh Nasuhidehnavi and Taylor M. Clark, 14 October 2026, Annals of Pharmacotherapy. DOI: 10.1177/10600280261494015

#6503. Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds

Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes arenât good at telling the full windy story - they canât tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.

Earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones. Weâve also seen them on Venus, Titan, and, surprisingly, Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Each is made up of different materials, but all share a crucial characteristic - their âsandâ consists of small grains of similar particles, which could be blown around by wind.

Understanding why this is important requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place. When air is moving across a dune, individual grains stay stationary until the wind itself reaches a critical speed known as the transport threshold. Once it rises above that, the grains begin bouncing across the ground in a movement known as saltation. Each time a grain crashes back to the surface, it kicks up other surrounding grains into the air, creating a self-sustaining cascade of moving sand.

Fraser talks about whether Martian dust storms are dangerous.

What was unclear to scientists was whether these motions were primarily driven by violent dust storms that were relatively rare, or moderate winds which are much more common on the other worlds where dunes have been seen. It might seem counter-intuitive that a comet would have âwindâ, but a 2017 study showed that the âripplesâ ESAâs Rosetta probe found on the comet's surface were created by localized vapor flows caused by extreme day-night temperature cycling.

Solving the mystery of what type of wind causes these shifting sands was the focus of the paper. Lead author M. Colin Marvin, a PhD student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford, collected wind speed data and detailed grain-size measurements from twenty-four different dune fields spread all over the world. From the Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah to the ancient, hundred-meter-tall dunes in the Namib Sand Sea in Namibia, the researchers found a remarkable similarity.

Across every terrestrial site, the most sand was moved when the wind was slightly above the speed required to start moving it. And, crucially, the same relationship also held on a Maritan sand dune. The process didnât require the odd violent gale to get sand moving, just every day wind speeds common throughout the globe. For example, a dune made of sand 0.2 mm across (about the width of two pieces of paper) is mostly moved by winds blowing at only 26 kilometers per hour 10 meters above the ground.

Fraser talks about the Dragonfly mission, which will land next to dunes on Titan.

With that data set in hand, the researchers then turned to simulations. Using a tool called ReSCAL, they grew virtual dunes from flat sand beds using different wind speeds. As part of that process, the team confirmed that, as long as a world has plenty of loosely bound grains of sand and winds that grow rarer as they grow stronger, dunes will largely be formed by the wind speeds that correspond directly to the grain sizes that compose them.

Despite the challenges of finding individual sand grain size from orbit, this technique is useful on more than just Earth. Curiosity has already drilled into the Stimson formation, a layer of sandstone that used to be a windblown dune billions of years ago. Another upcoming interplanetary mission â Dragonfly â is expected to touch down on the surface of Titan, where there are dunes of hydrocarbons, sometime in the 2030s.

Combining the grain size measurements from these missions with the math laid out in the new paper will provide scientists with a rough indication of the history of wind speed in the area. There will also undoubtedly be other missions to other dune-ridden planets - Venus comes to mind as a potential target. And from now on, scientists will be able to read a major part of a worldâs geological history directly written into its sand.

Stanford - Scientists discover sand dunes can reveal wind speeds on Earth and beyond

M. Colin Marvin et al - Windblown dunes are born in sand at the brink of transport [Author's note - PNAS page not fully indexed at time of writing]

UT - Interpreting Dune Patterns: Insights from Earth and Mars

UT - Compare Sand Dunes Across the Solar System, From Venus to Pluto

#6502. The 6 Most Reliable Walkie-Talkies for When You Need Them Most

Stay connected wherever you go with these durable, two-way radios built for everything from backcountry trips to emergencies.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When it comes to backcountry safety, there’s no messing around. Serious adventure seekers know it’s best to prepare for their outdoor escapades—whether they’re heading deep into the wilderness or staying close to home. If not, you risk injury or worse. From a reliable fixed-blade knife to a solid pair of binoculars for scouting the trail ahead, there’s a whole slew of gear to keep you safe outdoors.

Used for decades, walkie-talkies are a lesser-talked-about gadget for hikers, campers, paddlers, bikers, skiers, and more heading into the wilderness. Yet this humble piece of equipment plays an important role in helping you communicate with colleagues, friends, and family when you’re on the go. They’re also a smart backup in an emergency and a way to monitor the weather in untamed landscapes and far-off places.

Today’s walkie-talkies haven’t changed all too much in look and feel from their early days. But they’re nothing like the cheap, toy versions we used as kids when exploring backyard “wilderness.” Modern features like NOAA weather alerts, VOX (hands-free operation), and app-connected features provide safeguards and peace of mind—especially in faraway places.

Our guide below covers what to keep in mind and how to choose a walkie-talkie for work, play, and emergencies—and offers a closer look at standout models worth your money.

Our evaluation process combined rigorous field testing across a wide variety of walkie-talkies in different environments with extensive research from trusted online sources. Meehan’s in-field testing for his best two-way radio picks ranged from trekking deep into the backcountry on hut trips to communicating seamlessly while mountain biking to traveling around a city.

Recognizing that walkie-talkies serve a wide audience, we also considered other scenarios where dependable communication is essential—on construction sites, inside expansive venues like convention centers, and across large retail operations.

With this breadth of uses in mind, we reviewed models spanning a range of functions and price points, carefully weighing usability, durability, range, features, and cost. For radios we couldn’t test directly, we reviewed trusted sources and compared specs. We also factored in real-world customer feedback, ensuring our final selections reflect not only expert insights but also everyday user experiences.

These Midland radios have proven reliable in the city and the mountains. The two-pack is a great value and includes advanced features like hands-free VOX and NOAA weather channel monitoring.

It's one of the most versatile walkie-talkies in terms of power options. As part of a two-pack, you get a charging cradle for each, but you can also charge the device with a micro-USB cable and, if you’re in the field for multiple days and run out of power, you can switch the battery pack out for a new one or use three AA batteries to power it—though it is hard to get the cover off.

The radios are compatible with multiple accessories, like a hand-held mic-speaker or an earpiece-mic combo. The latter makes hands-free use even easier, like in a restaurant or store setting.

But in the end, this relatively affordable set of walkies has an ideal feature set for most people.

It shouldn’t surprise that a company known for its smartphones, like the Razr+, would add smartphone-like features to its top-line walkie-talkies. That’s exactly what Motorola did with its 800-series Talkabout line.

It uses the Talkabout app for iOS and Android devices to enable features other walkie-talkies can’t, like letting you use the 800 series as a sort of smartphone modem when there’s no cell service.

The app also lets you send texts or share your location with others using an 800-series radio and the app. This feature is unavailable on most walkie-talkies, since they’re just two-way radios. It also supports smart pairing and connects to Bluetooth devices, like headphones or earbuds.

Most walkie-talkies on the market are waterproof, or at the very least water-resistant, since they’re meant for outdoor use. But you’ll find it harder to find a two-way radio that can actually float. That’s where Cobra's floating walkie-talkies stand out.

Built to IPX7 waterproof standards, this radio can survive full immersion underwater and is designed to float—ideal for situations like water sports, boating, paddling, skiing, and backcountry adventures. This walkie-talkie can handle dunkings and wet environments where communication is critical, and its orange rubber exterior makes it easy to spot in choppy surf or on snow-covered slopes.

Best for whitewater kayakers, stand-up paddle boarders, or even families enjoying a long weekend on the boat, it's a solid pick when you want to stay connected without worrying about waterlogging. You won’t have to worry about sinking or failing when wet. This durability is also ideal for backcountry skiers or climbers who deal with wet conditions daily.

Extra features like voice-activated transmission (aka hands-free talking) and the ability to replay missed radio calls also pack a punch. With its 37-mile range, NOAA weather alerts, and an impressive 2662 channel combinations, this Cobra radio is more than just waterproof—it’s an essential tool for adventurers heading into rugged, remote environments.

In the end, it’s hard to deny the Rocky Talkie Mountain Radio's capabilities compared to others made for outdoor adventure. It could easily have been our top pick, but since not everyone goes on multi-day backcountry trips, the Mountain Radio is likely overkill for most.

Founded in 2019, RockyTalkie is a newcomer to the scene, but it has nailed it with this 2-watt FRS radio with great range. Even in forested, mountainous areas, we could still easily communicate over miles. It also had one of the longest-lasting batteries, even in freezing weather.

The Mountain Radio sports a really simple interface with just five buttons, and it’s easy to lock onto a channel. The radio also has a great speaker and microphone for transmitting and receiving calls and a bright green LED display that disappears when the radio isn’t actively transmitting or receiving.

We also appreciate the radio's rugged, rubberized outer shell and its two removable attachment points. The device uses carabiners rather than belt clips like most other two-way radios. That makes it easy to attach to just about anything—a harness, a belt loop, a backpack strap, a PFD, and more. The secondary attachment point uses smaller carabiners and a coiled leash, making it even harder to drop or lose.

The only thing we found lacking in the radio is that it can’t scan and play NOAA weather alerts, which would be very helpful in a backcountry setting with no access to cell service.

The Rocky Talkie 5-Watt Radio showcases backcountry endurance at its finest. It’s beefed-up, replaceable battery lasts up to six full days on a single charge. That’s nearly a week of reliable communication without scrambling for a power bank or solar panel to plug into while off-grid—making it one of the longest-lasting walkie-talkies in its class.

This two-way radio also shines for its durability, with an IP67 waterproof and dustproof rating. It also includes NOAA weather alerts, dual-frequency monitoring, and up to 5 watts of transmitting power for extended range. An important note: you need a GMRS license to operate this radio legally in the field.

While its design is compact, it’s heavier than many other walkie-talkies we tested. That said, for the peace of mind that comes with extended battery life and a durable design that tops our list for its rugged, waterproof build, you can’t go wrong with this radio.

Bottom line: the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt is our go-to choice for lasting power and rugged dependability.

While it’s technically not a walkie-talkie, the Garmin InReach Mini 2 deserves a spot in any serious communication roundup. For backcountry adventures where two-way communication is less frequent or a walkie-talkie just won’t cut it, this pocket-sized satellite device becomes a lifeline—especially when cell service and radio coverage fail.

The InReach Mini 2 uses the Iridium satellite network to deliver global coverage wherever you roam. You can send two-way text messages, share GPS location, and trigger SOS alerts from literally anywhere in the world. This piece of tech is best described as a satellite phone stripped down to the essentials: sending and receiving messages without overcomplicating communications.

It weighs a mere 3.5 ounces, and its compact design lets you clip the sat-phone to your pack or strap, or slide it into your pocket. You can also sync the InReach Mini 2 with Garmin’s Earthmate app for easier texting if you have your phone with you on your adventures.

Another big selling point of this piece of gear over walkie-talkies is its 14-day lifespan—long enough for extended off-grid trips. Unlike FRS or GMRS walkie-talkies, which are limited by terrain and line-of-sight requirements, this communication device promises to keep you in touch with family and friends wherever your adventures take you. Even more importantly, it keeps you connected in an emergency.

While a walkie-talkie is a simple, handheld, portable two-way radio, not all are the same. Some are designed for indoor use, while others are meant for outdoor use. Some suit adventurers and sportspeople, while others offer features best suited to first responders. And, of course, some are designed for kids. When selecting the right two-way radios for your needs, there are plenty of factors to consider.

Most walkie-talkies are Family Radio Service (FRS) units with 2 watts or less of broadcasting power. These need no license. Devices that have more than 2 watts of broadcasting power, up to 50 watts, are called General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) units.

GMRS devices require an FCC license. However, as the folks at Rocky Talkie explain on their site, it’s pretty easy to get one online in the U.S. It costs $35 and is good for 10 years, covering everyone in your immediate family. The higher the wattage, the more transmitting power and range the walkie-talkie has, which generally means it uses more power and has a larger antenna. You can see that difference pretty clearly between the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt Radio and the brand’s smaller 2-watt Mountain Radio.

Both types of units can broadcast on a range of channels, and each channel has wattage restrictions. Channels 1 through 7 can broadcast at up to 5 watts. Channels 8 through 14 can only broadcast at up to 0.5 watts. Channels 15 through 22 can broadcast at up to 50 watts, making them ideal for communications up to 30 miles apart in good conditions.

Not all two-way radios are designed with the same level of user-friendliness and a simple interface. The interface plays a big role in how easy the device is to use, especially when in the field with limited bandwidth for fidgeting with buttons and screen controls. Some radios keep things simple with large knobs and backlit buttons that let you seamlessly switch channels or adjust volume with a quick twist or tap—even while wearing gloves. Others rely on small digital menus that can be challenging to navigate, especially while on the go.

And some advanced walkie-talkies even require setup, such as programming frequencies through a computer and cables. While this may give more control, it can intimidate newer two-way radio users.

When comparing radios, pay attention to details like clearly marked buttons, backlit displays for night use, and easy setup processes. Features like one-touch scanning or memory recall can be great options when you need quick, efficient communication. Ultimately, the best radio delivers reliable performance without sacrificing user experience—especially when it matters most in the field.

Most two-way radios use replaceable batteries, usually AA or AAA, rechargeable batteries, or sometimes can use either. Units with rechargeable batteries are often more expensive, but usually have good longevity for trail and backcountry use. Some units recharge in a cradle but ideally also have a port for charging via a DC or USB cable, allowing you to power up from a backup battery as needed. We’ve left units on overnight before and still had power in the morning, and some will go into a low-power mode when left on. The battery will last longer if you use the walkie less or use a lower wattage mode, but that will also reduce its transmitting and receiving range.

Obviously, you want your devices to last a long time, and walkie-talkies should endure for years and withstand knocks and drops. That's why most don’t have touchscreens or even glass screens. Most should be able to withstand minor spills or rain, but if you know you’ll be using them primarily in the water, like on a fishing boat or white-water rafting and kayaking, you’ll want a walkie-talkie that’s waterproof and carries an IP67 rating or higher. If you’re using walkies in the backcountry or on a job site, you’ll want two-way radios that are ruggedized—like the DeWalt 2-Watt Heavy-Duty Walkie-Talkie or Rocky Talkies—and can withstand drops better than some others.

Walkie-talkies offer a few options for remote operation. Some will allow VOX or hands-free operation and are activated by your voice. Others have wired microphones and speakers that are handheld or worn on a lapel or shoulder strap. Others have an earpiece and microphone. Some modern walkie-talkies can actually pair with Bluetooth earpieces, also allowing for hands-free communication. This is great when wearing a motorcycle helmet or when a wire could get in the way of whatever you’re doing.

Some models have additional channel monitoring or communication capabilities, like operating on two frequencies at the same time. These are handy features, but using them will drain the battery faster while they’re on.

Walkie-talkies designed for outdoor use, for example, can monitor NOAA weather channels, giving you some insight into the weather and the conditions you may face while camping, driving off-road, hiking, or hunting that you otherwise wouldn’t be able to access.

Still others can communicate and monitor two channels at the same time. That could allow you to communicate with multiple teams at once. For instance, in a rescue situation, you could communicate with your friends on one channel and the local sheriff’s office or the search-and-rescue team on another without switching channels every time.

While all walkie-talkie channels are open to all users, some are generally used by certain groups and/or in certain areas. You can talk with local organizations to find out which channels they use and broadcast on.

To help people connect with like minds, some are encouraging what they call community channels. These help people in a local backcountry area communicate with each other. Rocky Talkie lists some active community channels for local areas. While these channels help in some situations, you also don’t want to communicate constantly on channels monitored by SAR or local sheriff’s offices, because you could interrupt emergency operations.

Walkie-talkies come in a wide range of prices, and more expensive models often offer more benefits and features. So, while you can get a serviceable pair for about $30-$35, they won’t have much range or additional features. For a top-tier single walkie-talkie with multi-channel monitoring, high wattage and range, and water- and shock-proofing, you can expect to pay over $150 per unit.

Range is one of the biggest selling points for walkie-talkies, but it’s also one of the most misunderstood. Sure, the box may say “up to 35 miles of range.” That’s only if conditions are near-perfect—think one person on a mountain peak and another down in a valley, with nothing but clear air between them. In reality, terrain, obstructions, severe weather (like a snowstorm), and more can drastically cut that range. Dense forest, rocky canyons, massive hills, and buildings can shrink that range even more.

Most consumer FRS models perform best up to five miles, depending on the terrain. For most outdoor adventures, a reliable one-to-five-mile range is typical and usually enough to keep track of groups across rivers, campsites, or trails. GMRS radios, which we mentioned require a license, can stretch much further than five miles, especially when paired with repeaters.

Our recommendation: Shop for a walkie-talkie model and range based on realistic expectations for your use case, not the maximum range advertised in the brand’s marketing.

It depends! How often and for how long do you plan to use your radio? Are you looking for a basic radio or one built to perform off-grid? Battery life depends most on design and how often you use it. Most walkie-talkies advertise a battery lifespan of eight to 20 hours of runtime, but those numbers assume moderate to infrequent use. Continuous transmission drains the battery much faster than standby mode.

For shorter day hikes and quick outings, you won’t have to worry much about your radio lasting more than a single charge. On longer excursions, opt for a walkie-talkie that can be charged via USB-C with an external battery pack, or that uses AA or AAA batteries. Simply put: Don’t trust what the packaging says. Instead, consider how long you plan to use the two-way radio and whether you’ll have a chance to recharge partway through a long adventure.

Many modern two-way radios offer more than basic push-to-talk functionality. NOAA weather alerts are especially helpful for backcountry safety, providing real-time updates on weather patterns and severe storms heading your way.

Another feature to look for is VOX—voice-activated transmission—which enables hands-free use. Paddlers, bikers, and skiers are prime candidates for VOX-equipped walkie-talkies when devices aren’t always easy to grab while in motion.

For simple day-hiking trail use or communicating with your family across the campground, simple models will work just fine. But on bigger adventures like backpacking into the wilderness and remote paddling, investing in a two-way radio with all the bells and whistles gives you peace of mind and the right tools when conditions are worse than expected.

Erica Zazo (she/they) is a Chicago-based freelance writer covering outdoor news, gear, and guides for Backpacker Magazine, Outside, and more. She’s a big fan of urban nature, exploring lesser-known trails and towns, and the Midwest. Follow her adventures on Instagram: @onecurioustrvlr.

Chris Meehan is an internationally published writer, author, and editor with more than two decades of professional experience. He has authored multiple adventure guidebooks with Falcon Guides and his work focusses primarily on the nexus between sustainability and outdoor adventure. He is an experienced gear reviewer, tester, and travel writer who has explored multiple continents.

Now in its 17th year, the Eater Awards recognize the year’s best new restaurants, bakeries, bars, dishes, and chefs in markets across the U.S.. More than 30 Eater staffers and contributors spent months traveling to 44 cities to weigh contenders on food, service, atmosphere, and the stories behind them. The prize? A tomato can trophy. The night started off strong with photos at the tomato can-wrapped step-and-repeat and a welcome shot of Zbiotics, before guests headed up to the roof of Nine Orchard for panoramic views and more fun. #6500. A Major Review Reveals Three Antidepressants That May Outperform Prozac

A massive review of 30,000 people suggests three antidepressants may outperform Prozac, but the findings reveal how much remains unknown about long-term depression treatment.

A new review has found that some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found that people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta), and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

Treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an important part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

If, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants, so it’s important this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Studies of real-world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

The new review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

The findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

The findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

This means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six studies followed participants for longer than six months.

This means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is important given the average time people take them is much longer.

Importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

People respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

For someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

Continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

Ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects, and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing, or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.

Adapted from an article originally published in The Conversation.
