#6451. The 6 Best Office Chairs for All-Day Comfort and Support

Need a better seat for your workspace? We have your back with these recommendations.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Your 40-hour work week is much easier on your joints and back if you’re sitting in the right office chair. For better or worse, the office chair might be the most important piece of furniture you own, given the sheer number of hours you spend sitting and working each day. An office chair that properly supports your back, neck, and shoulders can turn what could be a painful week into a comfortable one.

That said, a good office chair has to be a lot more than comfortable. Unlike loungers or couches, office chairs require upright support that promotes good posture for your back and neck. They also need to be flexible and mobile enough to move with you throughout a full work day, whether that’s leaning back during a quick break or rolling across the floor to grab something from the printer.

Choosing the right office chair means considering your body type and how long you sit at your computer or gaming desktop on an average day. Check out our list of the best office chairs for support and comfort, plus a few essentials to consider before you make your final decision.

We researched options across several major online retailers and compared their key specs, design, and adjustable features. We also looked at opinions from reviewers, real-life buyers, and users on online discussion forums such as Reddit. After narrowing our list to a few dozen qualified options, we pared it down further based on price and availability. Regardless of your budget or personal tastes and needs, you should be able to find a comfortable office chair.

This Branch office chair is modern, with an understated design and solid support features. What sets it apart from other options here is its six points of adjustability. That includes adjustable lumbar support to improve posture and prevent fatigue, and a back that tilts and locks for a more relaxed position.

The chair’s firm, cushioned base is slightly curved at the front and back to support a more natural seated leg position. The seat also adjusts forward and backward.

Considering the customizable settings for comfort and support, this office chair is a far better option than any others at this price point.

The Staples Dexley’s headrest slides up and down and tilts to line up with the back of your head. You can also move the lumbar support to match the curve of your lower back. The seat and back are both mesh, so you'll stay cooler on a long workday than you would in a padded chair.

The Dexley uses a synchro-tilt mechanism, which tips the seat and backrest together when you lean back. A tension knob sets how hard you have to push to recline, and the tilt lock holds the back in one of three positions. The seat height runs from 17.4 to 21 inches, and the armrests move up and down. The seat depth is fixed, though, so you can't slide it forward or back to fit your leg length. Staples says the chair can support up to 275 pounds over a 5- to 10-hour workday and covers it with a 5-year limited warranty.

The Hon Ignition 2.0 has a lumbar pad that moves up and down the backrest to meet the curve of your lower back. The pad is hard plastic, and a few Amazon reviewers said it pressed into their backs harder than they liked. The seat slides forward and back. That lets you set how much of your thigh the seat supports, whether your legs are long or short. The armrests change in height and width.

The back is mesh, which lets air through and keeps you cooler over a long workday. Hon rates the chair for 300 pounds. The Advanced Synchro-Tilt version on this listing lets you adjust how much force it takes to recline and lock the back in place.

Lock in and play all night long with this Secretlab gaming chair. With supreme comfort and all the standard adjustability features of office chairs, this model has a notably high back and wide sides for extra support. Its adjustable lumbar moves both up and down as well as in and out.

Because intense gaming requires focus, the chair must fit your body and posture closely. That’s why this chair, unlike any other on our list, comes in multiple sizes. The gaming chair also comes with a magnetic pillow you can attach anywhere on the back for extra comfort.

If you need extra head and neck support, this office chair is worth a look. The adjustable headrest cradles the back of your head and neck to help prevent strain and fatigue. The chair is covered in a breathable nylon mesh fabric that’s easy to wipe clean.

Other highlights include armrests that adjust in three different directions, plus it offers good lumbar support with adjustable height and width. The office chair also locks in a reclining position for sturdy yet relaxed support.

Most office chair armrests go up and down, and that's it. The Gesture's rotate a full 360 degrees, so they can swing in under your forearms when you're typing and stay there when you lean back to scroll on your phone. The back curves to follow the S-shape of your spine instead of pressing flat against it. Steelcase also built air pockets into the seat cushion, which it says ease pressure when you're sitting for hours.

You don't have to stand up or lean over to adjust the Gesture. All the controls sit on the right side of the seat. From there, you can slide the seat forward or back, set how hard you push to recline, or lock the back upright. The recline stops at three positions.

The Gesture holds up to 400 pounds, more than any of our other picks. The weak spot is the lumbar support. It's built into the back and doesn't adjust on this version. If lower-back support is your main concern, our lumbar pick gives you more control for much less.

A good office chair must be both ergonomic and supportive. Ergonomic design promotes good posture and keeps your body in an optimal position for focusing and working. Ergonomics and good posture go hand in hand with quality lumbar support. Office chairs with good lumbar support feature curved or cushioned backs that align closely with the natural curve of your lower spine, keeping you comfortable and upright for long stretches. Some office chairs have air pumps or adjustable curvatures to tailor the chair closely to your body.

Getting the right fit in an office chair depends on its adjustability. Most swivel and roll chairs have adjustable pneumatic bases that raise and lower the chair so your legs stay at a flat, comfortable level. Along with these basic features, some office chairs have an air pump for customizable lumbar support or attachable cushion straps or neck rests, and height-adjustable armrests that slide side to side.

Office chairs are typically made of polyester, leather, or cloth, plus foam. Most polyester or plastic chairs have lightweight, breathable mesh seats and backs that still offer solid lumbar support. Leather and cloth office chairs are typically cushioned for a bit more give. Foam gently molds to your body and may be more comfortable for your legs and back than mesh office chairs.

A factory worker experimented with a pressurized air system while on the job, and it resulted in a fatal injury.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 35-year-old man in the Czech Republic

The symptoms: The man was injured while working in a factory. His co-workers learned he'd been hurt after he crawled from the ground floor to the first floor and shouted for help. He had severe abdominal pain and rectal bleeding, and he said he had been injured while conducting "a silly experiment" involving a pressurized air system. However, he did not describe exactly what had happened.

"He repeatedly stressed that the incident was his own fault," doctors later wrote in a report of his case.

What happened next: The man was flown by helicopter to a nearby hospital, but during the flight, he became unresponsive and showed signs of hemorrhagic shock — a type of shock caused by significant blood loss over a short period. Shock, broadly, is when organs and body tissues don't receive enough oxygen due to decreased blood flow; if untreated, it can lead to organ failure and death.

Medical attendants in the helicopter worked to revive the man, but he died before he could be admitted to the hospital. Because the fatal injury occurred at the man's workplace, the police ordered a medicolegal autopsy, which both identifies the cause of death and collects details for law enforcement agencies, as part of an inquest procedure.

The autopsy: The coroner examined the body and noted that the soft tissues of the man's face were swollen and abnormally distended from retained air. The man's anus and genital areas were similarly distended and densely coated with dried blood, with radial tears in the skin surrounding the anus.

Next, the coroner conducted an internal examination. The man's brain was swollen, and he had air bubbles in his brain and chest cavity. Blood had collected around his diaphragm (the large muscle that helps inflate and deflate the lungs). It had also accumulated in the wall between the heart chambers on the left side, in tubes leading to his lungs, and in the membranes covering his lungs and heart. Reservoirs of blood also pooled in the man's abdominal cavity, in the tube leading to his right kidney, and in his digestive organs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The man's heart was "shrunken and empty," according to the report.

The autopsy also revealed foreign objects stuck between loops of the man's small intestine. These included three pieces of a black rubber pipe stopper and scraps of a plastic bag. His rectum — the final straight portion of the large intestine — had detached violently from his anus. It was surrounded by blood and marked with a laceration that was nearly circular, indicating that an "explosive rectal injury" had triggered hemorrhagic shock and caused the man's death, the coroner concluded.

Further investigation: Additional evidence from the factory and rubber fragments in the man's small intestine provided the police with further insight into his injuries; additional clues came from his internet search history, including photos of himself that he'd submitted to an amateur sex website.

The police concluded that the man had been performing autoerotic anal stimulation while at work, using a rubber inflatable pipe stopper measuring 2 to 3 inches (50 to 70 millimeters) in diameter, and an air gun, a handheld device for directing powerful jets of compressed air.

They suggested that the man likely attached the expandable pipe stopper to the muzzle of the air gun, which was in turn connected to the factory's air distribution system by a long, high-pressure hose. He then covered the pipe stopper with a plastic bag, inserted it into his rectal cavity, and pressed the air gun's trigger, causing "an unexpected abrupt inflation and explosive bursting of the pipe stopper within his rectum," the doctors wrote in the case report.

What makes the case unique: This case is the first recorded example of a person dying from a "rectal explosion during self-gratification," the doctors wrote. Piecing together the circumstances leading up to the man's injury was important for the hospital's doctors and law enforcement to understand how the fatality likely occurred, the authors said.

When performed responsibly and consensually, rectal insertion of foreign bodies typically does not cause significant injury, the authors added. However, "the introduction of some objects into the rectum might have unpredictable and even fatal effects."

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Hejna, P., Zátopková, L., & Janík, M. (2020). Rectal explosion: A strange case of autoerotic death. International Journal of Legal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00414-020-02344-7

#6449. As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their big wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”

“The most important lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their plans could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”

Meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the new session.”

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

The group isn’t alone in floating a new approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a new precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who said he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

And Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

None of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he said, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the new Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”

But it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of New Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”

“The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he said.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6448. The 9 Best Dishwashers of 2026

Our top recommendations from Bosch, Whirlpool, Midea, and more can knock out dishes with minimal disruption.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’re tired of scrubbing pots and pans by hand, a good dishwasher is one of the best investments you can make for your home. The latest dishwasher models are smarter, quieter, and more efficient than previous generations, with soil-sensing cycles that adapt to your load, adjustable racks to accommodate dishes of all sizes, and quiet motors that won’t disrupt movie night. It’s the same kind of quality-of-life upgrade you get from buying a washing machine. Once you have one, it’s hard to imagine life without it.

Whether you’re replacing an aging unit or adding one to your home, the best dishwashers can make your kitchen routine easier. They may even help you save money on your water bill, too. To help narrow down your options, we focused on aspects like reliability, cleaning performance, and drying power, so your dishes come out spotless and ready to put away.

Adding a dishwasher to your home is an important decision, especially since it’s something you’ll be using a few times per week. To find the best models, we researched the top-rated machines from trusted brands like Bosch, Whirlpool, and GE, analyzing customer feedback and consulting expert reviews. We also relied on previous Popular Mechanics testing and extensive research to weigh the features that matter most in daily use.

Specifically, we prioritized quiet operation (favoring models under 50 decibels that won’t interrupt a conversation), adjustable racks and foldable tines, and proven cleaning performance. We then cross-referenced these insights with long-term reliability reports to ensure every pick on this list is built to last.

For our most recent update, we revisited the current dishwasher landscape to ensure every recommendation still holds up. We added new picks that offer a strong value, smart features, and a great fit for specific needs, like compact kitchens and busy households. We also re-evaluated our existing selections to confirm they remain competitive on price, performance, and availability.

The Bosch 300 Series checks all the right boxes as a top dishwasher. This front-control model cleans thoroughly with seven cycles, and it uses sensors and targeted spray arms to track soil and adjust as it runs. It’s quiet at 46 decibels, so you can run a cycle anytime without it interrupting your dinner conversation.

Storage is flexible, too. You get a standard third rack for utensils and other small items, plus a middle rack that adjusts to nine positions to make room for pots below and stemware above. Fold-down tines on the upper and lower racks accommodate lids and other cookware, and all three racks move smoothly. It also uses a condensation system for drying and leak protection that can automatically stop water intake if it detects a possible leak.

Other features include the ability to control and monitor cycles from your phone and hands-free voice control when paired with Amazon Alexa or Google Home. We only wish it had an auto-open door drying feature to top it all off, but this isn’t a major con by any means.

For around $500, the Frigidaire top control dishwasher is a dependable, modern dishwasher that offers Energy Star efficiency, a quick wash cycle, and a DishSense feature that helps adjust the wash based on how dirty the dishes are.

Meanwhile, Frigidaire’s Maxdry feature cranks up the heat for noticeably better drying than most entry-level models, so you’re not hand-drying half the load afterward. The fingerprint-resistant stainless steel finish also does a nice job of hiding smudges, helping it look cleaner for longer. It has a child lock, delay start, and a removable silverware basket, rounding out a feature set that feels surprisingly robust for a budget pick.

At 52 decibels, it won’t compete with high-end models that offer quieter performance, but it’s perfectly acceptable at this price point.

This dishwasher has nearly everything you want: a third rack, an adjustable second rack, and a handful of cycle options to thoroughly clean your dishes, including a quick wash and a high-temperature wash that helps remove grease. It also offers enhanced, fan-powered drying technology that ensures your cookware doesn’t come out damp. At 51 decibels, it’s not the loudest, but not the quietest either.

Other notable features include a presoak cycle to clean off stubborn food and folding tines to fit larger items like mixing bowls and large pots. Unfortunately, there is no WiFi support or app compatibility, limiting the dishwasher’s convenience compared to other models.

Dishwashers are more flexible than ever with multiple racks and ample space for efficient organization. This Midea top-control model stands out with a third rack and spray arms for each level, making it easy to customize the interior to get thorough cleaning.

You can raise or lower the middle rack by up to 2 inches to make room for big pots, baking sheets, or tall plates below, so you don’t have to go through the effort of hand-washing cumbersome dishes. The Midea also features a dedicated third rack for utensils and flat cooking tools, along with jets that spray directly into reusable water bottles.

Beyond organization, a three-stage drying system combines heated dry, auto-open door, and air circulation, so you’re not toweling dishes off after the cycle finishes. And with a 47 decibel sound rating, it runs quietly enough that it won’t disrupt conversations. The only thing we noticed was that some reviewers had complaints about the latch on the door rusting, and the racks breaking. That said, it may be less reliable in the long-term compared to higher-end models.

If you actually want the “smart” part of a smart dishwasher to pull its weight, this LG model is an easy standout. We like that WiFi and LG’s ThinQ app let you fire up or pause a cycle from the couch, check how much time is left, and get pinged when it’s done, while Alexa and Google Assistant support hands-free control. The app keeps an eye on water supply, drainage, and leaks, and sends alerts if something looks off. It also nudges you when it’s time for routine maintenance.

The smart features extend to how it runs, too. A sensor wash cycle automatically adjusts time and water based on how dirty your dishes actually are. LG’s one-hour wash and dry program also uses four multi-directional spray arms for deeper cleaning and then circulates heated air throughout the tub for faster drying.

An auto-vent feature pops the door open slightly at the end of a cycle to vent steam, and a status light projects onto the floor so you’re able to see when it’s done at a glance. These features combine to make cleaning your dishes a little smarter and less painful.

While the upper rack gets fold-down tines for odd-shaped glassware and bowls, the lower rack doesn’t, so it’s a bit trickier to load large pans and bakeware than on models with fully flexible lower racks. However, if you normally hand wash large pots and pans, this may not be an issue.

The Whirlpool Eco Series 24-Inch Top Control Dishwasher is a great pick for families that go through dishes like a small restaurant. It’s built to keep up with real-life cleanup, using a three-rack layout so you can load more dishes in one go. Below, the lower rack has fold-down tines for bulky cookware, making it easier to run a full day’s worth of dishes.

The Sensor cycle uses AI technology to monitor soil level, load size, and water temperature, then adjusts as it goes. There are also cycles that add soak time and longer wash phases to help reduce the need for pre-scrubbing. A sanitizer rinse option targets food-borne bacteria, while a high temperature wash helps cut through grease. Meanwhile, the combination of heated and condensation drying features mean you’ll have dishes that are ready to put away when the cycle finishes.

There is no app control or remote monitoring features, but this dishwasher does offer a fingerprint-resistant stainless exterior and a relatively quiet sound rating of 47 decibels. That means you’ll be able to throw it on without ruining family movie night.

The GE Profile 18-Inch Top Control Built-in Dishwasher is great for smaller apartments where cabinet space is tight. It offers full-height racks, an adjustable upper rack, and room for everyday dishes, glasses, and cookware. With a three-level wash system, you don’t have to pre-wash anything in the sink. It even features a cycle that automatically adjusts time and water based on how much dirt it detects on your dishes.

The GE also features a stainless steel tub, an ADA-compliant low-profile design, and a sound rating of 47 decibels, so you can run it while you’re watching TV without having to raise the volume. There is no third rack, but it does have fold-down tines and a removable silverware basket, providing you with more flexibility when loading dishes. As someone who dealt with a basic 18-inch dishwasher at a previous apartment, the GE is a big upgrade.

The Midea 18-Inch Built-in Dishwasher is a great budget pick if you want a true built-in dishwasher in a small space without spending a premium price. At 18 inches wide with room for 8 place settings, it tucks into narrow apartment kitchens, bar nooks, or RV islands while still handling daily dishes for a small household.

You get six wash settings, including Heavy, ECO, and Quick, plus heated dry and a sanitize option. The stainless-steel tub feels more durable and premium than its price suggests, and users call out how quiet it is while running. The main trade-offs are a somewhat fussy lower rack for full-size plates and long normal-cycle times; however, if you’re prioritizing price, small-footprint installation, and solid cleaning over bells and whistles, this Midea is an excellent and affordable option.

Sometimes you don’t feel like washing a small amount of dishes by hand, but running a full cycle on a dishwasher feels like a waste of energy and water. This double-drawer model from GE is here to try to solve that problem.

You can run the two drawers separately or together, whether you need a quick rinse for a few plates and glasses, or a deeper clean for multiple place settings. This is especially convenient because you can continue loading dirty dishes while the other drawer runs through a cycle.

The dishwasher has six wash cycles, plus sanitizing and extra dry options. There are four adjustable shelves per drawer to accommodate plenty of dish and glass sizes. The detergent compartment is a little harder to fit pods, so you may be better off with a liquid or powder cleaner.

Some dishwashers might have to be hardwired to a dedicated circuit rather than using a plug-and-play connection. Hardwired dishwashers are more secure and permanent, while units with power cords are easier to install and offer more convenient disconnection in case of repairs. Both styles require access to a 120-volt, grounded outlet. Check the specs of the dishwasher you’re considering to ensure it aligns with your desired connection type.

Most households will be fine with a standard built-in dishwasher that slides under the counter and hooks into existing plumbing. However, portable and countertop models have come a long way and are now legitimate options for renters and small kitchens. Options like the GE Portable Freestanding Dishwasher, roll to the sink when needed and store away when you’re done.

Meanwhile, countertop dishwashers live on a counter or sturdy cart, and are ideal for smaller spaces like studios, where a full-size unit may not fit. Just know that compact models often compromise on features like noise reduction and capacity due to their smaller size.

For most households, dishwashers generally come in two widths: the standard 24-inch and the compact 18-inch. A 24-inch model is usually the best choice for families, having enough room for bulky cookware and larger loads. In contrast, an 18-inch model is a space-saving solution for small kitchens or narrow cabinet cutouts. I used an 18-inch machine in a previous apartment and found it filled up fast, forcing us to run cycles more frequently.

Manufacturers like to quote capacity in “place settings,” but what really matters day to day is interior flexibility and vertical space. Look for a tall tub design, which maximizes interior height so you can fit oversized items like baking sheets and pots on the bottom rack. A model with a third rack and an adjustable second rack, like the Whirlpool Eco Series Top Control Dishwasher, will give you enough flexibility to wash an entire day’s worth of cookware in a single load.

One of the biggest differentiators between modern dishwashers and older models is noise, which is measured in decibels (dB). Anything around 50 decibels or below is generally considered very quiet and shouldn’t overpower a normal conversation. Standard units that produce sound at around 51 decibels are more noticeable, especially during spray and drain cycles.

If you’re particularly sensitive to noise or often run the dishwasher at night outside of your energy company’s peak hours, look for models that promise quieter performance. Many of the newest dishwashers run quietly enough that you’ll barely notice them in the background. There have been multiple times when I’ve opened my Samsung dishwasher at home mid-cycle because I didn’t hear it running.

One of the most frustrating parts of using a dishwasher is opening the door to find wet dishes. Fortunately, modern dishwashers utilize several methods to ensure they come out bone-dry.

Some rely on traditional heated dry cycles, which raise interior temperature to evaporate moisture. Others take a more energy-efficient approach called condensation drying, where residual heat from the hot rinse water evaporates moisture against the cooler stainless steel walls. Newer models, like the Midea 24-Inch Top Control Built-in Dishwasher, have an auto-open feature, which automatically pops open the door at the end of the cycle to vent steam and ensure that even plastic containers dry completely.

Modern dishwashers pack more features than ever. When shopping around, you’ll see things like third racks for utensils, height-adjustable upper racks, soil sensors, foldable tines, and WiFi and app control. Many of these features give you the flexibility to load your dishes more efficiently, which means you can wash more items in a single load and are less likely to need to rewash plates or glasses.

Also consider where a dishwasher’s controls are (hidden on top versus front-facing), whether the tub is stainless steel, and other things that could potentially enhance your experience. Just remember that every added feature usually nudges the price up. Whatever you buy, make a habit of cleaning your dishwasher a couple times per year to keep it running like new.

Most households will be fine with a standard 24-inch dishwasher, which offers enough room for everyday dishes and larger cookware. But if you’re working with a smaller kitchen or apartment, an 18-inch model saves valuable real estate. “Your choice depends on available space, how many dishes you typically wash, and the size of the pans you cook with,” says Glenn Lewis, president of Mr. Appliance, a Neighborly company.

Yes, and it’s worth checking before you buy. “They need a dedicated 120-volt electrical connection, a water supply line, and a drain connection, all of which must meet local building codes for safe operation,” Lewis says. If you’re replacing an existing unit, the connections are likely already in place, but if you’re adding a dishwasher for the first time, you may need to hire a professional to set up the plumbing and electrical.

It’s possible, but proceed with caution. “You can if you have basic plumbing and electrical knowledge, but improper installation can lead to leaks or electrical issues, so many homeowners opt for professional installation,” Lewis says. If you’re swapping out an old unit and the connections are already there, a DIY install is more manageable. But for a first-time installation, professional help is usually the safer bet.

An Energy Star certification means the dishwasher meets strict efficiency standards that might save you money over time. “Energy Star-certified models use less water and electricity, not only to run the dishwasher but to heat the water used by the dishwasher,” Lewis says. “Lower energy means lower utility bills and reduced environmental impact over time.” If you’re choosing between two similar models, going with the Energy Star-certified option is usually the smarter long-term investment.

In her free time you can likely find her trading trinkets at an EDM festival, searching for hidden gems at thrift stores, or cuddling with her two cats.

A 2,000-year-old tomb was discovered in an elite burial ground of the Xiongnu, some of whom were the ancestors of the Huns.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed a massive 2,000-year-old tomb of an elite nomad from the Xiongnu Empire in Central Asia. The nine-level tomb contained more than 400 grave goods and is the largest Xiongnu tomb ever found in Mongolia.

Archaeologists identified the enormous tomb full of riches during a four-year excavation at the site of Duurlig Nars in northern Mongolia, according to a translated statement from the National Museum of Korea, whose researchers have been excavating the site in cooperation with the Institute of Archaeology of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia.

Duurlig Nars is the largest noble burial complex of the Xiongnu Empire, with nearly 300 ancient burial mounds called kurgans. The Xiongnu, also known as the Hunnu, were a collection of nomadic tribes who coalesced into a mobile empire on the Mongolian steppe in 209 B.C. The Xiongnu were connected to a broad trading network that stretched from the Roman Empire in the West to China and the Korean Peninsula in the East.

When the Xiongnu Empire fractured in the late first century B.C., one band moved west, picking up new tribes and eventually becoming the horde known as the Huns. Both the Xiongnu and the Huns were well known for their fighting and horseback riding skills.

The newly announced tomb is roughly square, with a long passageway extending from it, according to the statement. Including the passageway, the tomb is about 240 feet (73 meters) long, roughly the size of the Great Sphinx of Giza. Archaeologists discovered nine concentric layers of stone, each smaller than the last, going down around 48 feet (14.5 m) deep, making the tomb a kind of inverted pyramid.

Jade "bi" discs unearthed on the floor of the coffin.

A glass cup with a handle, possibly made in the Roman Empire.

Archaeologists unearthed a wooden carriage from one of the tomb layers.

In the tomb's central chamber, archaeologists found a wooden burial chamber with a coffin. The burial chamber is smaller than other elite Xiongnu burials, according to the statement, which may suggest that the society was changing and Xiongnu power was declining when the tomb was created in the late first to second century A.D.

Artifacts found in the tomb show the extent of the Xiongnu's connections across Eurasia 2,000 years ago, according to the statement. Among the grave goods recovered from the tomb were silver-and-quartz accessories crafted to decorate horses, as well as a wheel from a lacquered horse-drawn carriage, suggesting the tomb's occupant was a person of high social status.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Additionally, archaeologists found evidence of connections with the Han dynasty, which arose around 200 B.C. and was the second imperial dynasty of ancient China. On the bottom of the wooden coffin, archaeologists recovered 15 flat, overlapping pieces of jade.

Han dynasty burials of important people often included at least one "bi," the term for a jade disk. But unlike the typically circular "bi," the jade pieces in the Xiongnu tomb are irregular and have elaborate designs engraved on them, according to the statement. This may suggest that the Xiongnu adopted a Han burial practice but put their own spin on it.

Archaeologists also found a broken cup in the tomb. The transparent glass cup with a handle may have been manufactured in the Roman Empire, the archaeologists believe. Additional tests will be carried out to try to determine where the glass cup was made.

So far, archaeologists are unsure who was buried in the tomb. But they plan to use DNA analysis techniques on the teeth and hair they recovered from the coffin to figure out the person's chromosomal sex and whether the individual was related to other people interred in the Duurlig Nars burial complex. According to the statement, future analyses of this important tomb will help archaeologists paint a more detailed picture of ancient Xiongnu society two millennia ago.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6446. Meeks vows Iran votes as he seeks Foreign Affairs gavel

Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and staffers cheer as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., takes the stage during a election night watch party in Washington on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., the presumed next chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, plans to bring resolutions to the floor to “immediately” end the war with Iran when Democrats take control of the House in January, he wrote in a letter Thursday seeking his colleagues’ support to become chairman.

The letter, which officially announced his bid for the chairmanship, lays out his oversight agenda for the committee, which will also see considerable turnover on the GOP side of the dais.

Meeks and other Democrats have repeatedly forced votes this year on war powers resolutions seeking to end the Iran war, with a Meeks-sponsored one clearing both chambers of Congress.

But those resolutions have been nonbinding concurrent resolutions, since the 1973 War Powers Resolution only lays out a fast-track procedure the minority party can wield for concurrent resolutions in the House.

With a House majority, though, Democrats could bring binding joint resolutions to the floor.

Beyond war powers votes, Meeks also promised public hearings on the war. He also vowed hearings on a range of topics including the administration’s Venezuela policy and “repeated defiance of Congress's constitutional authority over war powers and trade.”

“As chairman in the 120th Congress, oversight of this administration’s lawlessness and corruption will be at the top of the agenda,” Meeks wrote. “I will continue to advance a principled foreign policy grounded in our values, including support for Ukraine against Russian aggression.”

In addition to Iran measures, Meeks also promised legislation focused on “clawing back Congress’s proper role in the making of American foreign policy” and a State Department reauthorization bill that puts guardrails on the administration and protects career diplomats.

Meanwhile, the GOP side of the committee is poised to lose at least a dozen lawmakers — or about half of its members — next year between retirements and election losses.

The departures include longtime members such as former Chairman Michael McCaul, R-Texas, who opted not to seek reelection, and Rep. Scott Perry, R-Pa., the Freedom Caucus chair who lost his reelection race.

Several other Republican committee members remained locked in races that were still too close to call as of Thursday afternoon, according to The Associated Press, potentially gutting the GOP committee bench further. They include GOP Rep. Young Kim of California, the East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee chair who was trailing her in race against fellow California Republican Rep. Ken Calvert.

Rep. Christopher H. Smith, R-N.J., who chairs the Africa Subcommittee, lamented the turnover Thursday but predicted a lot of interest among remaining House Republicans to fill the void.

“There will be many who will want to be on it,” Smith told reporters. “We lost some really great people. Yesterday I can't tell you how sad I was about friends who are now not coming back.”

#6445. The 8 Best Cordless Stick Vacuums Are Convenient, Versatile, and Work Well on Carpets Too

These lightweight, easy-to-store models get the job done with multiple attachments and powerful motors.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A cordless stick vacuum has the potential to be one of the most convenient cleaning tools in your home. These lightweight machines make it easy to clean up pet hair from area rugs and hidden dust along baseboards, without having to haul out an upright vacuum or wrestling with a power cord. Most models also convert into handheld vacuums, giving you more flexibility to clean furniture, stairs, and other hard-to-reach spots.

Suction power, battery life, maneuverability, and dustbin capacities vary between models, so the right cordless stick vacuum ultimately depends on your home’s flooring, how much debris you’re dealing with, and the features that will actually make your cleaning routine easier.

We’ve rounded up the best cordless stick vacuums worth considering based on our hands-on experience, with options for everything from everyday maintenance to deeper carpet cleaning.

🔎 Looking for more ways to keep your floors and furniture clean? Check out our stories on the best robot vacuums, the best vacuums for pet hair, the best vacuums for hardwood floors, and the best handheld vacuums.

I’ve spent considerable time researching, testing, and vetting all types of vacuums, so I’ve developed a pretty good understanding of what separates a genuinely useful appliance from one that is just going to take up space in your storage closet. I’ve evaluated a wide range of models, including full-size uprights, canister vacuums, robot, and handheld models vacuums, paying close attention to performance, ease of use, and features that can really make a difference in a your regular cleaning routine.

When testing cordless stick vacuums, we assessed how well each model could handle common household debris, its ability to transition between carpet and hardwood floors, and how easy it was to move around furniture and into tighter spaces. We also looked at the practical considerations like battery life, suction power, dustbin capacity, weight, filtration, and included attachments.

Beyond just how the vacuum cleans, we also considered the overall experience for an owner. Removable batteries, self-cleaning docking stations, washable filters, and easy-to-empty dustbins can also make daily vacuuming less of a drag. The below recommendations are both powerful and dependable for a wide range of cleaning needs and surface types.

The Dyson V15 Detect is the most expensive stick vacuum in our lineup, but if you can stomach the price tag, you’ll get a cordless stick vacuum that (quite literally) leaves the competition in the dust across the board. It delivers top-notch performance on floors and carpets to tackle everything from fine dust and pet dander to larger debris.

Its motor spins up to 125,000 rpm and it comes with two cleaning heads, including an upgraded version of the brand’s “fluffy” head that features a green laser headlight to detect fine dust. During testing, we found that being able to switch from cordless to handheld made it easier to transition from tackling small messes to deeper cleaning sessions.

The auto mode is a nice feature for conserving battery life, as this model only runs for about an hour off one charge. Another highlight is the motorized pet tool.

Full Dyson V15 Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

The PowerClean FurFinder is a more affordable alternative to the PowerClean FurGuard we recommend, but that doesn’t mean you have to give up useful features.

This cordless stick vacuum is intended for use on a variety of floor types, and the flat-lay construction makes cleaning under furniture much more accessible. The vacuum also stands up on its own which leads to fewer interruptions during a cleaning session.

We love that both the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment come with headlights because it makes it a lot easier to see hidden dirt and debris. The brush roll is a tangle-free design, and the FurFinder is equipped with a HEPA filter for trapping small particles and allergens.

The motor on this vacuum is less powerful than the PowerClean, but it still provides plenty of suction for daily household cleaning.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurFinder Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Since we’re big fans of the Shark AZ2002 Vertex upright vacuum for deep and thorough cleans, it’s no surprise that we like the cordless model in this lineup, too. The brush roll is excellent at pulling hair and large debris from carpets, as well as polishing up your hardwood floors. The cordless stick vacuum features an advertised runtime of 60 minutes.

It also offers a HEPA filtration system and converts to a hand vac, and it also bends at the center of the wand to get around and under furniture. The Vertex comes with plenty of accessories for cleaning a variety of spaces. However, this may not be the best choice if you regularly clean stairs, as the cordless vacuum weighs roughly nine pounds—significantly more than other vacuums we cover.

I have two cats and live with my partner, which means there is plenty of mess to go around, from pet hair and dust to tracked-in dirt. I appreciate all the thoughtful features of the Tineco Station 5 because they make daily maintenance much easier.

Automatic suction adjustment has proved useful on my laminate and tile floors. I can hear when the motor gets a boost of power in a particularly dirty area, and it helps on carpets and area rugs where crumbs and debris tends to get trapped between the fibers. Add to that a green laser light for dust detection and you’ll hardly ever miss a spot.

I particularly like the base station. It has a 2.5-liter capacity, and after two months of using the Station 5, I still haven’t had to empty it. When I dock the vacuum onto the base, it automatically empties the onboard dustbin, cleans the floorhead brush roll, and charges the vacuum. Combined, these intuitive features make for a cleaning routine that is virtually hands-free.

Full Tineco Pure ONE Station 5 Pro Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Even though the Dyson V11 Origin came out several years ago, that doesn’t mean this model has stopped being useful.

The motorbar cleaner head works exceptionally well on carpet, successfully agitating fibers to pull up embedded dirt, dander, and hair. Suction is equally impressive, and there are three power modes depending on the level of cleaning you need. I ran the vacuum on medium most of the time, but I used boost occasionally whenever an area needed the extra attention.

This model doesn’t come with a soft roller brush vacuum head, and while it does work on all floor types, it can be loud on hardwood and laminate. But if your home is mostly carpet, this is a cordless stick vacuum I would reach for.

Full Dyson V11 Origin Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Our tester has a busy household six pets, so there’s no question that she’s regularly cleaning up after her animals. Pulling out the upright vacuum daily isn’t convenient, so she turned to the Levoit LVAC-300 to fill the gap.

This cordless stick vacuum has three different cleaning modes—eco, medium, and max—and she was able to cycle through each right from the handle depending on how much suction power she needed. She found that the vacuum was able to pick up litter and sand on different surfaces and between thresholds with ease.

The attachments are useful for cleaning curtains, cushions, and staircases, but she was disappointed that there’s nowhere to store these tools on the vacuum itself. The LVAC-300 runs for up to 60 minutes depending on what mode you’re using, and the HEPA filter is a great feature if you have animals.

Full Levoit LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

I used the Bissell PowerClean FurGuard across my apartment to clean laminate floors, area rugs, carpeting, and upholstery, and I fell in love with several features.

The vacuum lays completely flat, making it really easy to get underneath furniture, and the swivel steering helps guide the FurGuard around tight spaces. Being a pet owner, I appreciate that the brush roll is tangle-free, so I don’t have to cut hair loose as often as I would with a standard, bristled brush roll.

Other highlights were lights on the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment. I was able to see collected dirt and debris that I would normally miss on hardwood flooring, carpet, and furniture. I also like that this model is designed to be self-standing.

It’s hard to come by a cordless stick vacuum that you don’t have to re-mount or set on the ground during your cleaning session. With this model, I was able to stop and start with ease.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurGuard Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

We recently got our hands on one of the latest cordless stick vacuums from Shark, and we were impressed by the PowerDetect’s construction. The pole has a hinge in the center and when you release it, the vacuum bends to extend under furniture and hard-to-reach places. Our tester didn’t have to kneel down or adjust angles while he was cleaning thanks to the intuitive design.

Beyond that, the PowerDetect vacuum uses sensors on the bottom of the floor head to discern between surface types, and adjusts suction power when needed. During testing, the motor could be heard transitioning speeds when used on hardwood and shag carpet.

This vacuum also comes with a docking station, which automates the process of emptying out the dustbin. The vacuum itself can’t hold that much debris onboard, so it’s nice having a one-stop-shop for clearing out the bagless canister during a cleaning session. It’s a little heavy for a cordless stick vacuum, but it still gets the job done.

Full Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Not every cordless stick vacuum we test ends up in this roundup. However, these other models still perform well and are reliable recommendations:

Levoit Aero Cordless Vacuum Cleaner: The Tineco we’ve included above has more raw suction power, reaching up to 27,000Pa versus the 14,000Pa of the Levoit. However, one of the highlights of the Aero is the 3.5-liter-capacity dust bag in the docking station. Depending on your cleaning frequency, you could potentially go months without having to empty and replace it, and this design is better for keeping dust and dander from being expelled back into the air.

Dyson Gen5Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum: This cordless stick vacuum certainly commands a premium price, and you get a lot of the same features as the Dyson V15 Detect we recommend above, such as an LCD display screen, the Fluffy Optic cleaner head, and pet hair attachments. If you’re an allergy sufferer, you may prefer the Gen5Detect because its filtration system captures particles down to 0.1 microns, while the V15 filters down to just 0.3 microns. Plus, runtime is slightly longer on the Gen5Detect.

The main advantages of owning a cordless stick vacuum are easy portability and storage. But what you trade for the convenience is battery life and runtime. Most models clean from 30 to 60 minutes, but that’s also dependent on what setting you’re using. If you’re running the vacuum on its highest speed the entire time, it might die faster. Be wary of manufacturers’ advertised total runtime because it may represent performance on the lowest setting or using two fully charged batteries, for instance. Battery charging should also be factored in, so plan your cleaning session accordingly so you don’t lose power in the middle of a floor swipe.

Like we mentioned earlier, the dustbins on cordless stick vacuums are significantly smaller than those of an upright or canister unit. You should consider your cleaning habits and the spaces you usually vacuum to find a model that aligns with your needs. If you live in an apartment or are using the cordless vac to supplement your other cleaning supplies, then a dustbin with at least half a liter capacity should do. Some of the models we recommend hold up to one liter of debris, which helps limit the number of trips to the trash can.

Although not a necessity, having a good amount of attachments with your vacuum is especially helpful for cleaning hard-to-reach places or targeting specific issues. Crevice tools pick up dirt and dander from corners and couch cushions, while bristled brushes and motorized pet tools agitate and lift hair and fur that’s been embedded into upholstery.

A good filtration system helps combat allergens such as dust and pet dander that are being kicked up by a vacuum. The best option is a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter, which traps 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. A fully sealed or multi-step filtration system also has the potential to trap a wide variety of airborne allergens without releasing them back into your home.

Cordless vacuums are very effective at picking up pet hair, especially models designed with high suction power and specialized brush rolls. Some of the models we recommend include motorized attachments that lift embedded hair from upholstery and carpets. Anti-tangle vacuum heads are also a key feature that helps prevent hair from wrapping around the brush roll. While not all models perform equally, a high-quality cordless stick vacuum is able to handle pet hair just as well as traditional versions.

The lifespan of these vacuums typically lasts from three to five years, depending on usage, build quality, and maintenance. Battery performance plays a major role, since lithium-ion batteries start to lose capacity over time.

Avoiding overcharging and storing the vacuum properly could help extend the battery life significantly. Running regular maintenance like cleaning the vacuum filters and emptying the dustbin completely preserves suction and functionality. Higher-end models often last longer due to better materials and replaceable parts, but either price point has potential to last for years with proper care.

Modern designs are increasingly more effective at cleaning many surface types, including rugs and carpets. Advances in battery tech and general efficiency have allowed for strong suction performance that is comparable to corded models. Adjustable power modes allow for deeper cleaning on thicker carpets, and multi-roller and motorized brush heads agitate fibers to loosen dirt and debris.

Performance may vary depending on the type of flooring. Some vacuums are designed to work on low-to-medium pile carpets, while others are able to handle high-pile. It’s best to consult the listed features and specs of the model you’re considering to ensure it aligns with the flooring types in your home.

Biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas lifts the lid on the secret life of tardigrades in stunning detail for the Nikon Small World photography awards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's not often we get to peer into the tiny world of tardigrades (also known as water bears). But through his photography, biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas is unmasking the secret lives of these creatures in stunning detail.

In one photo, which won Quiroga-Artigas 12th place in Nikon's 2026 Photomicrography Competition, a tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is seen shedding its tough outer layer, known as a cuticle or an exuvium, while laying an egg in the discarded skin.

"A large part of my research involves imaging, and during the many hours I spend at the confocal microscope, I have come across some incredibly beautiful and unexpected scenes," Quiroga-Artigas, a postdoctoral researcher at the Montpellier Cell Biology Research Center in France, told Live Science in an email.

"An interesting feature of tardigrade reproduction is that some species lay their eggs inside the shed cuticle, or exuvium. The exuvium can therefore provide an additional layer of physical protection for the developing embryos."

In some species, males may place sperm inside the cuticle of a molting female before egg laying, according to National Geographic. In others, the males fertilize the eggs after they have been left inside the cuticle. And some don't even need males to reproduce at all.

"Many species reproduce through parthenogenesis," Quiroga-Artigas said, which is when an embryo develops from an unfertilized egg, also known as a virgin birth. "This means that males are not required for reproduction, and the resulting offspring are genetically very similar to their mothers," he added. The species in the photograph falls into this category.

Molting and egg laying often take place over several hours, but the shedding itself is a relatively fast process. Capturing it on camera is, therefore, no mean feat.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Once I had collected animals that were laying eggs, I had to fix, stain, and mount the specimens before imaging them," Quiroga-Artigas said. "I then spent a long microscopy session searching for the right specimen and the right orientation to obtain a high-quality image. Finding a specimen at exactly the right stage of molting, and in an orientation that allows the process to be clearly visualized, is largely a matter of patience and luck."

—Tardigrades survive being dried out thanks to proteins found in no other animals on Earth

—Tardigrades may hitchhike on snails ... and then suffocate in their slime

—'Sexy Mantis,' obscene orangutan and prancing sparrowhawk feature in 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards

Photographing these animals is also challenging due to their tiny size. "Working with tardigrades in the lab requires a lot of experience with micromanipulation, as they are extremely small," Quiroga-Artigas said. "Hypsibius exemplaris, for example, is only about 250 µm [micrometers] long." That's about twice the width of a human hair.

This particular photo was taken using confocal microscopy, which uses a focused laser beam to light up one section at a time to create a detailed, high-resolution image. Quiroga-Artigas used this technique for a second tardigrade photo that was listed as an Image of Distinction in the same competition.

The second image submitted by Quiroga-Artigas to the Nikon Small World competition of a tardigrade shown from beneath.

He also received an Honorable Mention in the Nikon Small World in Motion Competition for a video of a pregnant tardigrade making contact with another tardigrade, which can then be seen pooping. However, it's not clear whether the contact between the two individuals caused this movement, Quiroga-Artigas said.

Quiroga-Artigas hopes his photography and videos give viewers an idea of just how beautiful and complex the microscopic world really is. "There are tiny animals all around us that we cannot see with the naked eye, yet they live, reproduce, grow, and undergo complex life cycles just like the animals we are more familiar with," he said.

"I will continue capturing images of tardigrades in different contexts related to my future research, without necessarily having a specific photographic goal in mind," he added. "In my experience, some of the best images I have captured were not necessarily the ones I was actively looking for."

Pandora is the trending news editor at Live Science. She is also a science presenter and previously worked as Senior Science and Health Reporter at Newsweek. Pandora holds a Biological Sciences degree from the University of Oxford, where she specialised in biochemistry and molecular biology.

#6443. How 4 states voted on election-related ballot measures

Maryland voters fill out ballots at a polling site in Bowie on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.

Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:

Voters in Maryland on Tuesday approved an amendment to the state’s constitution that will make it easier for the state’s Democrat-controlled legislature to redraw the congressional map for the 2028 elections.

The outcome was a victory for Democrats, who could potentially eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held seat – the 1st District on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, represented by Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of the hard-line conservative House Freedom Caucus.

The Old Line State emerged as a bright spot in Democrats’ plan to counter the redistricting wars initiated by President Donald Trump and turbocharged by the spring Supreme Court ruling that diluted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and set off a slew of Republican-led map-remaking across the South.

But those GOP-led efforts appeared to backfire this week, with Democrats holding many of the redrawn seats in states such as Texas, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina.

Still, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told reporters Wednesday that he was “ready to engage” with the legislature on a new map, citing the threat of further redistricting in Republican states.

“Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states, to go after places like Mississippi and South Carolina and Indiana,” Moore said, according to video posted by WBAL-TV 11 News.

Following an unsuccessful attempt to redraw the Maryland map in February, Moore called a special August legislative session during which state lawmakers voted to put the redistricting amendment, known as Question 3, on the November ballot.

The move faced immediate legal challenges from Republicans. Two Maryland courts ruled to block the measure from appearing on the ballot, finding that lawmakers had missed the legally imposed deadline to refer the ballot measure. The state’s Supreme Court, though, allowed the redistricting amendment to go before the voters, with changes to the ballot text.

State and national Democrats campaigned heavily for Question 3 as some public polling pointed to skepticism among voters. Former President Barack Obama even appeared in an ad urging voters to approve it.

Voters in the Show-Me State overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map that sought to dismantle a safely Democratic seat in the Kansas City area.

Missouri Republicans enacted the new lines in 2025, aiming to give them an advantage in seven of the state’s eight House districts, including the 5th District held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver II.

A protracted legal and political tussle over the map ensued.

The group People Not Politicians Missouri started a citizen petition to put the adoption of the map to a statewide vote. While the petition effort was pending, the state held its August primaries under the new lines. But in September, the state Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 map could not be used in the general election because of the pending ballot measure and ordered state officials to hold November’s election under the previous boundaries, first enacted in 2022.

Attempts to challenge the ruling in federal court ultimately proved unsuccessful, with the U.S. Supreme Court issuing an order that reinstated the 2022 map.

Groups on both sides of the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, reportedly spent millions to persuade voters. But St. Louis Public Radio reported last week that while opponents of the 2025 map were actively campaigning against it, organized efforts in favor of Proposition A appeared “nearly nonexistent.”

Republican efforts to try again and enact a new congressional map for 2028 could be complicated by a constitutional amendment, approved by voters Tuesday, that curtails the power of state legislators to override the result of a voter-approved initiative.

Voters in Massachusetts opted this week not to join states such as California and Washington and adopt a nonpartisan primary system.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, would have replaced the state’s partisan primaries with an open primary under which all candidates would appear on the same ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to the general election.

The outcome was a victory for the chorus of labor unions and progressive groups, including the Working Families Party, that opposed the measure. Holding so-called jungle primaries, the groups argued, could make it harder for candidates without financial resources or high name recognition to run for office.

A bipartisan coalition that included the NAACP of New England and Republican former Gov. Charlie Baker supported the measure, arguing that open primaries would give voters more choice and create more competitive elections in a state dominated by Democrats.

Alaskans weighed in this year for the second time as many cycles on a ballot measure to revert to partisan primaries and repeal the state's top-four ranked choice voting system.

With over 70 percent of the vote in, The Associated Press had yet to call the ballot initiative, known as Measure 2, which would also roll back certain campaign finance disclosure requirements. As of Thursday evening, the “no” side, which supports keeping the current election system, was narrowly ahead. The state has until Nov. 18 to finish counting outstanding ballots.

Under Alaska’s voting system, all candidates run on the same ballot during the primary. Then the top four candidates, regardless of party, advance to the general election, which is decided by ranked choice voting if no one takes a majority of the vote.

In 2024, Alaska voters narrowly voted to keep the current system in place.

National Republicans, though, have largely opposed ranked choice voting, including Trump, who has characterized Alaska’s voting system as a “scam.”

The state’s use of open primaries and the top-four ranked choice system has drawn fresh scrutiny this year.  Outside groups spent big sums trying to boost underdog candidates during the Senate primary in an effort to hurt the front-runners. And several candidates in the Senate, House and governor’s races dropped out before the deadline to finalize the general election ballot, again trying to prevent splitting votes with their party front-runners.

Then last week, the Senate race was upended by a New York Times investigation that revealed operatives aligned with the Senate campaign of Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate with a similar name to GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan in an attempt to stack the ballot with two Republicans with the same first and last names. The revelations have fueled an ongoing debate in the state about whether ranked choice voting encourages this kind of alleged campaign chicanery.

“We would not be having this conversation at all if we didn’t have a thing in place called ranked choice voting,” Mike Dunleavy, Alaska's outgoing Republican governor, told Fox News last week.

Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the revelations, as has the Justice Department. The DOJ also sought to block the certification of the Senate result if the incumbent Sullivan loses. Last weekend, a federal court dismissed the lawsuit.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states that currently use ranked choice voting in regular federal elections, along with the District of Columbia.

Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.
