#6428. Trump names Stephen Miller his chief of staff ahead of Dem takeover

Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, talks with reporters at the White House on April 28. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Stephen Miller, the architect of the hard-line immigration and deportation program voters rejected this week, will become White House chief of staff.

Susie Wiles will depart that post and move to the Trump political organization, which appears to be in full operation, even after the president's last midterm election. Miller has been deputy chief of staff, overseeing the Trump administration's domestic policy.

Miller’s first day will be Monday, Trump said in a social media post.

Trump dubbed Miller “one of my most trusted advisors” and said Wiles, who also oversaw his 2024 presidential campaign, “has done an outstanding job.”

Wiles, who Trump recently announced had won a battle with breast cancer, said in a X post that “serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding she was “proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

The chief-of-staff change came three days after Republicans were demolished in Trump’s final midterm election, with House Democrats on pace for the largest majority in over a decade and at least a 54-seat Senate majority come January.

Trump addressed the personnel move as he departed the White House Friday for an event and weekend in Florida — though he ignored a question about his recent declaration that Wiles would be sticking around.

“I wanted to make a change,” he said in a roughly three-minute exchange with reporters before he walked to Marine One. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”

Trump in recent days had become open to working with Democrats after the new Congress is seated on Jan. 3, even after railing against what he called the party’s “bad” policy during an October-long campaign rally blitz.

“Look, I mean, I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “But I have the power of the veto. So if we don't like what they're doing… They've already called and they want to talk about things. And that's fine.”

Trump summoned Thursday's press pool into the Oval Office for an executive order signing. On his desk was a red baseball cap with "VETO" across the front in large white lettering.

Miller has worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to several GOP lawmakers, including former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who became attorney general in Trump's first administration.

But making the hard-line Miller his White House chief of staff even before congressional Democrats get organized likely will draw the ire of the incoming majority.

Virginia Rep. Donald S. Beyer Jr. was among the first Democratic lawmakers to slam Trump’s decision.

“Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller doubles down on the politics of hatred, lawlessness, and failure that the American people soundly rejected three days ago,” Beyer said in a statement. "Miller embodies the worst elements of the Trump presidency. His promotion shows that Trump has learned nothing from his electoral debacle and has no intention of even trying to work constructively with the next Congress.”

Many congressional Democrats — leaders, returning incumbents and members-elect — want to investigate Trump, his inner circle and family members while also pursuing a legislative agenda aimed at paring the cost of living.

To that end, as chief of staff, Democrat-run committees calling Miller to testify is highly unlikely since he could continue to claim executive privilege. That allows senior White House aides to withhold many internal West Wing communications, documents, and presidential-related conversations and actions, from lawmakers.

In public comments and television interviews, Miller has accused Democrats of being aligned with figures and candidates who “hate” Americans, and once said the party is “unworthy of power.”

“So the Democrats have become a party of freaks, weirdos, losers and crazies,” Miller said during a July appearance on Fox News. “But you can’t laugh it off because it’s deadly serious. When you give these people power, everything you know and love in this world falls apart. You have chaos, corruption, decay, violence, poverty.”

#6427. The brain’s protective barrier also blocks medicine. This engineer wants a way through

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Laura Sanders

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Rebecca Pinals hadn’t planned to study neuroscience. But as she watched her grandmother decline from dementia, the chemical engineer decided to apply her talents to the human brain.

At the time, “one of the big questions was, ‘how do we get access to it?’” says Pinals, of Stanford University. “I thought nanotechnology could be an interesting and useful toolkit to answer those types of questions.”

One key access point is the blood-brain barrier, a dynamic microenvironment of cells that helps keep pathogens and other contaminants out of the brain. It’s so good at its job that drugs for treating dementia have a hard time penetrating it. It’s important for researchers to understand this barrier, Pinals says, but it is so thin and fragile that they can’t observe it in real time without risking patient health.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Pinals and colleagues re-created the blood-brain barrier on a microchip. The team reprogrammed stem cells engineered from human skin, then coaxed the cells to form the barrier in a small 3-D chamber on the chip.

“As an engineer, this [system] is perfect,” Pinals says. “We love to take things apart and put them back together to learn how it’s made.”

Experts could use this scale model of the blood-brain barrier to figure out how to noninvasively access brains affected by neurodegenerative diseases. Pinals wants to use the device to investigate nanoparticles that could deliver drugs directly to patients’ brains.

#6426. Brain scans reveal where fractions fit on the mental number line

Brain scans show that adults use a shared mental number line to compare fractions and whole numbers, even as the brain distinguishes between them.

A quarter looks more like four on the page, but its value is much closer to zero. In a new brain scan study, that difference mattered.

As adults compared fractions and whole numbers, brain activity followed a shared number line.

The patterns still distinguished fractions from whole numbers, but numbers close in value tended to produce more similar patterns.

One idea about how the brain handles abstract concepts is that it files related concepts close together, so that similar ideas produce similar patterns of activity.

Numbers are a good way to test that, because everyone agrees on their order.

Daniela Valério and Stanislas Dehaene of the Inserm-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit, known as Unicog, led the study at the NeuroSpin center outside Paris.

People have long been known to carry a number line in their heads for whole numbers. The team wanted to know whether fractions, which children learn after years of schooling, get added to the same line.

Twenty-two adults took part, all right-handed native French speakers between 19 and 39 who had finished high school with a science track.

Two were excluded, one for a cyst found on the scan and one who had a panic attack in the scanner.

That left 20 participants in the brain scan analysis. A faulty response button reduced the number to 19 for the analysis of speed and accuracy.

Each person lay in a high-field MRI scanner run by the French research agency CEA. The numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 and the fractions 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 3/2, and 5/2 flashed up one at a time, each for one second.

For every number, the person pressed a button to say whether it was bigger or smaller than the one before.

Each run lasted just under ten minutes, and every number followed every other number exactly once. The fractions were built from the same digits as the whole numbers on purpose.

That let the team tell whether the brain was reading 1/4 as a quarter or as a 1 next to a 4.

Fractions slowed people down. A comparison between two fractions took about 1.2 seconds on average, against 0.8 seconds between two whole numbers.

People also got 9.5 percent of fraction pairs wrong, compared with 3.7 percent of whole number pairs.

In an interview with Earth.com, Valério said fractions are harder for a few reasons.

Whole numbers follow a simple counting sequence, so 3 is followed by 4, while there is always another fraction between any two different numbers.

The size of a fraction is also not always easy to judge from the numbers in it. “For example, although 5 is greater than 3, 1/5 is smaller than 1/3,” Valério said.

Numbers that were close together were also harder than numbers far apart, whichever kind they were. The closer two numbers were, the slower and less accurate people got, and the effect was strongest when both were fractions.

Psychologists have known this distance effect for whole numbers for decades, and here it held for fractions too.

The team then laid out the speed and error data as a map. The 12 numbers fell along a single curved line in order of size, with the fractions among the whole numbers where their values belonged.

The scans showed the same thing. Across the brain regions that handle math, the pattern of activity for each number varied along two main directions.

One separated fractions from whole numbers. The other ordered all 12 numbers by size, from small to large, and ignored whether they were fractions.

The size ordering was strongest in the intraparietal sulcus, a fold near the top and back of the brain that has long been tied to math.

Researchers have also linked this region to the ability to estimate quantities. In the new study, patterns of activity in the hippocampus also reflected how close numbers were in value.

Then the team looked at single points on the cortex.

Within the front part of that parietal fold, many spots responded most to one particular number and less to its neighbors. The spots formed a map, with small numbers at the front and larger numbers farther back.

The map for fractions matched the map for whole numbers. Spots that preferred 0 also responded to 1/4, 1/3, and 1/2, and 1/4 ended up far from 4.

Valério said that when people compare numbers, they have to focus on magnitude, meaning how large or small each one is.

“Our study shows that the brain organizes this information into a shared map, much like a mental number line, “Valerio told Earth.com.

“This map brings whole numbers, such as 1 and 2, and fractions, such as 1/2 and 2/3, into the same system, according to their values.”

The size map showed up in only 14 or 15 of the 20 participants, depending on the number type. The fractions also stopped at 5/2, short of the range the whole numbers covered.

Fractions and whole numbers were mixed in one stream, so people may have had to build a single line to keep up.

The authors wrote that if the two kinds had been shown in separate sessions, each might still have run from small to large. The two lines might not have lined up, though.

Valério said the study was not designed to explain why fractions are harder to learn or to find the best way to teach them. Other studies in her lab are working on that.

Her next step is to see how the shared map differs across people with different mathematical backgrounds and levels of education, and whether those differences go with mathematical ability.

How the brain represents fractions in children who are still learning them remains an open question.

The team has posted its data and code on the Open Science Framework. It wrote that longer scanning sessions could extend the map to more kinds of math.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.

#6425. The 8 Best Refrigerators to Keep Your Food Fresh and Organized

We gathered the latest picks from popular brands like Samsung, Maytag, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A refrigerator is intended to do only three things: preserve food, store it properly, and supply enough lighting to see all contents. We also want our fridge to be reliable and last a long time so we don’t have to go through this exhaustive shopping exercise again until it’s absolutely necessary.

When shopping for a refrigerator, we're not just looking for something that keeps our food cold. We require aesthetic appeal from our primary kitchen appliance. We also crave convenience in the form of spacious and adjustable shelves and bins, temperature or humidity-controlled spaces, an ice maker so we can ditch the refillable trays, and whatever other clever additions fridge makers come up with to lure us into spending more cash.

If you haven’t shopped for a refrigerator in a while, we’ve got some good news and some bad news. The bad news is that refrigerators may be more expensive due to ongoing tariffs on both foreign steel and aluminum used to manufacture models in the U.S. and on wholly imported fridges. The good news, though, is that there is a wider variety of designs and sizes to match your family’s specific needs, plus features like exterior or interior water and ice dispensing options, separate food-specific cooling spaces, and an abundance of smart tech.

To help you find the perfect fridge for your kitchen, we researched a variety of options based on specific criteria and found the best of the best. We also made sure our picks all varied in terms of style, so below, you'll find our top recommendations for French door refrigerators, side-by-side fridges, and a number of other types, as well.

As with any other appliance, our consideration for best models was primarily based on value—capacity and features for the money. Value also incorporates the reputation of the manufacturer and opinions from both retailers and consumers (from online reviews). We also compared capacities and feature sets of various models and took into account our own hands-on experiences at appliance stores and trade shows over the years.

When faced with seemingly equal choices, especially on price, we always leaned toward higher-capacity models since we know there’s no such thing as too much refrigerator space. However, we also recognize that higher-capacity refrigerators are usually full or standard depth models that may be too big for many kitchens, so we’ve tried to add less pricey, smaller alternatives where we found them.

Stewart Wolpin wrote the initial version of this article—he's covered consumer technology, including home entertainment and appliances, since the early 1980s. Amber Joglar, a technology and home appliance editor with PM, handled the latest update to this roundup.

While there is a plethora of premium refrigerators priced $5,000 and up—and some priced $15,000 and more—we decided to keep our “Best” choices under $5,000.

If ensuring your food stays cool is at the top of your list when shopping for a refrigerator, then your best bet is investing in this four-door Samsung model. It's equipped with AI hybrid cooling, which essentially means using just electricity, sans refrigerant, via a semiconductor-based component.

This fridge automatically cools down to compensate for when you leave the door open too long. As a result, Samsung claims that meat and seafood are preserved a smidge longer, and your fridge’s overall power usage can be lowered by up to 10 percent.

Beyond this cooling technology, the Samsung offers plenty of convenient features. The beverage center inside the left top door provides a tall water dispenser, a 48-ounce autofill water pitcher with infuser, and a removable nozzle for cleaning. The dual ice maker behind the bottom left door makes both ice cubes and ice spheres.

The fridge’s doors open via gentle touch rather than forcing you to tug on handles, which is useful for when your arms are filled with groceries. You can also set the multi-pantry drawer for the correct cooling conditions to properly preserve fruit and veggies, beverages, or meat and fish.

This Samsung counter-depth four-door has a generous 22.5 cubic feet of capacity and 13.8 percent more cooling capability than previous comparable Samsung models.

This GE fridge is about as basic and uncomplicated as it gets, which explains why it only costs around $800 after discount. What makes this fridge a bargain is its substantial 21.9 cubic feet of storage space, which is more than a majority of other entry-level top-freezer fridges we considered.

One of its door shelves accommodates gallon jugs, and the included bins are modular to adjust to different jar, bottle, and container heights. Temperature controls are straightforward and easy to access on the roof of the fridge. It also includes a Sabbath mode to eliminate all the fridge’s electrical responses when the door is opened. Plus, it’s garage-ready.

This model is available in five finishes, but any colors other than white add to the overall cost. It also lacks both a freezer light and an ice maker, which means you’re going to have to fill and empty trays somewhat regularly.

But if you want to avoid an ice-making mess, you can buy an optional ice maker designed for this model, although it will occupy more than a third of your freezer space. (Or you could buy one of our favorite countertop nugget ice makers instead.)

This is one robust fridge for just $1,200. You get an impressive 27.4 cubic feet of total storage space in this full-depth Samsung stainless steel side-by-side, plus the interior ice maker is located in the door to create even more freezer shelf space.

Aside from being roomy, this fridge includes a raft of both cooling and convenience features normally found on more expensive models. For instance, it instantly lowers the temperature of your fridge and freezer section to quickly bring recently purchased goods to their appropriate storage levels.

The in-door water dispenser also dispenses both cubed and crushed ice, but it lacks a light, which makes it difficult to accurately fill a glass in a dark kitchen. There's an LCD panel on the inside of the fridge for monitoring refrigerator and freezer temperatures, ice maker filter status, and managing lock controls.

Multi-vent cooling lowers the temp in every corner of the fridge, which prevents ice-infused liquids. While it lacks some of the fancier frills of some of our other, more expensive choices, this Samsung provides a lot of storage space, especially in its freezer, for a relatively low price tag.

If it's even possible for a refrigerator to be entertaining, this French door LG does it and thankfully it doesn't skimp on functionality in the process. Right off the bat, you’ll notice a shaded window on the right door—just gently knock twice and it turns clear so you can take a peek inside. Then, grab the door just right, and a door within the main door opens with easy, quick access to snacks and drinks without letting all the cool air out from the main fridge compartment.

If you’re tired of old-fashioned ice cubes, freshen drinks with Craft Ice, an interior ice maker that fashions slow-melting spheric ice modules. The exterior water dispenser also makes both crushed and cubed ice, and the dispenser/ice maker mechanism inside the left door is thin enough to accommodate three door bins.

Unfortunately, the freezer is organized with deep, basket-style compartments, which makes it difficult to quickly find what you need in a pinch. But if you’re a frequent party host, the freezer really steps up the ice production, so you’re less likely to ever run out, even during a lively party.

There are side-by-side fridges with fancier features, but you'd be hard-pressed to find a better deal than this Whirlpool model, considering its combination of capacity, extras, aesthetic appeal, and overall cooling excellence.

This fridge has a spacious 28.7-cubic-foot capacity and is equipped with both an extra tall exterior water and ice dispenser to accommodate all sizes of glasses, bottles, and pitchers. The interior ice bin is installed on the door to free up freezer storage space. There's a good variety of glass shelves inside, and they extend wall-to-wall to truly maximize all fridge and freezer space available.

There is also a temperature management system that senses and adapts to keep food fresh. Special pantry and deli drawers maintain organization, too. If any foods have defrosted in between the grocery store and home, the freezer has a Fast Freeze option that quickly drops the temperature 10 degrees lower than the normal setting, so your foods can get back to fully frozen in a jiffy.

Unfortunately, if you’re looking to match this fridge with your kitchen decor, it's available only in a “stainless” finish.

This full-depth GE bottom freezer, which has been available since 2022, is still well-respected in its category, and it costs around $1,000 less than it was at first launch. Its enduring popularity can likely be attributed to its 24.9-cubic-foot capacity that’s generous for this class of fridge, although the water filter is unusually bulky and takes up a little more cooling space than we would have liked.

Fortunately, it includes an ice maker along with a larger-than-average storage bin—perfect for party preparation. A turbo cool setting automatically drops the internal temperature if the door’s been open too long. We also love the unique, horizontally-sliding snack drawer that easily moves across the fridge to make room for taller items below.

Other nice features include touch temperature controls, an open door alarm, and a fingerprint-resistant stainless finish. And, as found on most top- or bottom-freezer models, the top door is reversible, so you can install it to swing open left or right.

This model is also Energy Star-certified, meaning it meets strict standards set by the EPA and uses between 9 and 15 percent less energy than models that have not been rated.

Samsung makes arguably the smartest fridges around, particularly with its Family Hub models that integrate seamlessly into smart home ecosystems. The right door of this appliance boasts a 32-inch vertical touch screen that provides access to recipes, shopping lists, ordering, and other food-related tasks. In addition to these functions, it acts a streaming interface and display for your kids’ school drawings or home videos.

Inside, this fridge has a camera that recognizes and automatically labels 37 unobscured fresh food items such as fruits and vegetables, or you can do this manually. On the left side, there’s a double quick-access door. Behind that lives a beverage center designed with both a regular water dispenser and an auto-refill water pitcher with an infuser.

Open its doors either manually or automatically by touching a sensor. To better preserve different types of food, one of the freezer drawers lets you set one of five different temperatures depending on what you’re storing. A dual ice maker makes both standard cubes and smaller “ice bits,” but not crushed ice. An internal camera lets you see what’s inside your fridge—or not—when shopping via the smartphone app, which also lets you monitor the fridge’s power usage.

GE Profile appliances are considered high-end within the GE family, sitting above standard GE appliances but below its relatively expensive Monogram line. To put it simply, you get luxury features without a large price tag by investing in this model.

Inside the left of the four-door refrigerator is an auto-refillable water pitcher that doubles as a dispenser, and the bottom left freezer compartment contains roomy storage that holds a whopping 12.5 pounds of filtered ice. The bottom right can also function as a freezer, chiller, or fridge if you run out of space up top.

This fridge doesn't have an exterior water dispenser, but it does have a built-in pitcher with advanced filtration inside the left door. The door-in-door with rotating bin is a standout feature for us, too.

From a design POV, you get a smooth stainless steel exterior door finish with sleek handles, and the interior is highlighted by silver shelf and drawer trim handles, and an LED light wall. If you want to take advantage of smart features, the fridge has built-in WiFi and compatibility with the SmartHQ app for a fully customizable experience.

Each fridge form offers varying cubic-foot capacity, usually expressed as total space. Until recently, inside capacity was somewhat restricted by the need for refrigerant circulation and insulation inside a fridge’s thick walls. But many newer models with updated cooling and insulation technologies have slimmed these inside walls to create so-called “max,” “mega,” or “XL” capacity models, creating more inside capacity without increasing exterior dimensions.

Bear in mind, some vendors fudge on capacity, often rounding up to the nearest whole number in the name of the fridge. For instance, a “23” cubic foot model may actually only contain 22.5 cubic feet of storage.

So how do you decide how big your new fridge needs to be? Obviously, how much capacity you can buy depends on how much space you have in your kitchen for a refrigerator.

Figure 4- to 6 cubic feet per family member, leaning toward the higher end for a lot of shared items. Alternatively, you can start with ten cubic feet for the household, then add 1.5 cubic feet per household member to get a minimum capacity.

In terms of fridge-freezer split, most models assign 65 to 70 percent of space to cooling and the remaining 30 to 35 percent to freezing. If you’re a bulk buyer or frequent meal preparer, we recommend you find a model with more freezer space.

You want shelves and inside door bins to offer varying height adjustments to accommodate the tallest types of containers such as opened wine bottles. Some fridges offer shelves that slide out and door bins that can accommodate bulky gallon jugs or tilt out for easier access.

All refrigerators include storage drawers, but the best are those models that offer drawers with some sort of temperature and/or humidity control. When shopping, check the drawers to make sure they slide in and out smoothly, come out easily for cleaning, and don’t feel cheap.

Refrigerators with twin doors—side-by-side and French—are the only models in which you’ll find exterior in-door water and ice dispensers. Most in-door water dispensers also dispense ice—often both cubed and crushed—but some don’t offer ice, so double-check this before you buy. If a twin-door model doesn’t include an exterior water dispenser, there’s likely one inside the fridge.

If you’re replacing a fridge without an in-door water dispensing with one that does, you (or, more likely, a plumber) will likely first have to install a separate water line that connects from your under-sink pipes to your new refrigerator. You’ll also occasionally have to change the refrigerator’s water filter—usually around twice a year—but ask first to make sure of the timing. Our advice: order in a supply of filters so you’re sure you’re always dispensing the freshest filtered water.

A growing number of “smart” refrigerators include interior cameras to let you view your fridge’s contents to confirm if you need something while grocery shopping. A camera-equipped smart model with a smart screen on the door can also scan your remaining ingredients and create an edible recipe, assemble a shopping list and create an order from a grocery delivery service, and even identify what food items have reached their expiration date.

Yes, refrigerators still come in basic white, but you also can choose from a growing variety of subtleties such as gray and black tones in shiny or matte finishes (with smudge- or finger-resistant coatings). But a few fridge makers also offer custom-made colors, including finishes to match your kitchen cabinets or decor.

Do note that a model listed as having a “stainless” finish does not necessarily mean you’re getting an actual stainless steel door. In most instances, just the word “stainless” likely means the door is some other material, not stainless steel. To make sure you’re getting a true stainless steel door, first feel it, as stainless steel is cooler to the touch than other materials. Also, take along a refrigerator magnet—most stainless steel doors are not magnetic.

There are, essentially, only five forms of fridges, all defined by how the doors and drawers are arranged. In order of price, features available, and capacity (low to high), the five fridge forms are:

This is the most familiar no-frills fridge format with two doors: a top freezer compartment and a larger fresh food compartment below. Top freezer fridges are usually the least expensive fridge option, landing somewhere between $500-$900. They also range between 10 to 24 cubic feet of space, and are best suited for single folks or couples on a budget, or as a second fridge for a recreational basement or garage.

No frills means you’re unlikely to find any top freezer models with in-door water dispensers or an ice maker. Most models come with reversible doors that open left-to-right or right-to-left, however.

A.k.a. “bottom freezer” models, these refrigerators are equipped with a single door up top and a freezer drawer usually encompassing two shelving tiers below. Bottom freezer models are presumably more attractive to those with fewer freezer needs since you have to kneel or bend over to rummage through it.

Bottom freezer models generally provide a bit more freezer space than a top freezer— around 18 to 22 cubic feet of total capacity—and typically cost more than a top freezer model. Like a top freezer model, you’re unlikely to find bottom freezer models with in-door water dispensers, but some pricier versions do include ice makers.

Rather than a horizontal freezer, side-by-side models offer vertical freezing and cooling compartments. Side-by-side interior horizontal space, however, is narrower than a top- or bottom-freezer model, so wide platter trays or frozen pizzas may not fit. Side-by-sides are more likely to offer in-door water or ice dispensing, which can further reduce freezer space.

Essentially a side-by-side with a bottom freezer, except the two top French doors open out to reveal a single large and wide cooling compartment. Since there’s no wall dividing the top section, French door models offer the highest capacity—up to around 30 cubic feet worth of fresh food room—which makes these the best option for a large and active family.

French door models usually include either in-door or interior water and ice dispensers. Higher capacity, of course, means higher prices—French door models start at around $1,400 depending on interior space and features, such as more convenient separate dual freezer drawers.

Four-door French-door fridges replace the bottom freezer drawer(s) with freezer doors that open into separate compartments. However, you’ll see models with French doors with dual drawer freezers referred to as “four-door,” which they are not since a drawer is decidedly not a door. More expensive four-door models allow you to convert one of the freezer sections into an extra refrigerator compartment if you need extra cooling space.

Most refrigerators last around seven years. Spending a bit more now on a better model means you can go a lot longer without having to buy a replacement. Models with long warranties usually signal a longer expected lifespan.

Our general refrigerator shopping advice: you already know your current refrigerator’s shortcomings (that’s presumably why you’re looking to buy a new one). Match your known needs with the features outlined above that you find attractive before you go to a store and are confronted by a pushy salesperson.

It's not recommended to turn your fridge on and off for short periods of time because it can actually increase wear on the compressor, but powering down during longer absences helps save energy and prevents issues like mold.

Before heading out for vacation or an extended trip, you should remove all food, clean and dry the interior, unplug the appliance, and keep the doors propped open for air circulation.

He also serves as the unofficial historian for CTA (Consumer Technology Association), the trade group that produces the Consumer Electronics Show (CES), which he has attended and covered since 1984. He is also a huge Beatles fan and a METS season ticket holder.

Specializing in kitchen gadgets, small appliances, lifestyle, and consumer tech, she brings hands-on testing and a detail-oriented approach to every review. In her free time you can likely find her trading trinkets at an EDM festival, searching for hidden gems at thrift stores, or cuddling with her two cats.

#6424. Hawaii’s 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch was carved from lava that flowed about 550 years ago, and in late September it fell into the Pacific

The 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park collapsed in late September 2026. Here is how it formed and why sea arches eventually fall.

For years, visitors who drove to the end of Chain of Craters Road in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park could walk a short distance and see a 90-foot arch of lava rock reaching out from the cliffs into the Pacific Ocean.

That view is gone. The Hōlei Sea Arch was still standing on Wednesday, September 23, 2026. By the night of Sunday, September 27, it had collapsed into the ocean, the National Park Service announced on October 1.

The exact time of the collapse is unknown. According to the park, it could have happened while the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo.

The arch stood about 90 feet (27.4 meters) high and extended from steep sea cliffs into the ocean along the park’s southern coast, on the Island of Hawaiʻi.

It was carved into the cliff of an ancient lava flow from about 550 years ago, according to the park. The arch took shape through what geologists call differential erosion: some layers of lava are harder than others, so the sea wears them away at different speeds.

Visitors could see it by walking a short distance from the end of Chain of Craters Road, which the park described in 2020 as a 19-mile drive through some of the most spectacular scenery in the park.

The park’s own page on the arch was clear about one thing. The formation was beautiful but temporary, with a limited life span, and it would eventually crumble into the sea.

Sea arches like Hōlei can be found along a wide stretch of Hawaiʻi’s southern coast. They are remnants of once-continuous sea cliffs, built where lava met the sea and added to the size of the island.

Lava meeting the sea can even build whole new land, as it did when a new island rose from the sea off Iceland in 1963.

The moment that new lava cooled and turned to rock, it began to erode, the park explains. The seas on the island’s southern edge are known for rough water and violent surf, and the waves slowly break apart the rock and carve sea caves into the cliffs.

When waves hit the back wall of a sea cave, the water bounces back and starts to erode the cave’s headland. Over time, that forms an arch.

The erosion does not stop there. Given enough time, the waves cause the remaining bridge of rock to collapse, leaving behind a pile of rocks known as a sea stack.

Volcanic coastlines are constantly being remade, and on the same island, Kīlauea has produced 55 lava fountains since December 2024.

The coastline around the arch had shown signs of instability for years.

Earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea eruption and summit collapse damaged the cliffs near the arch. In January 2020, new cracks and instability led the park to close the original viewing area and the short trail to it.

“This new development reminds us that Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is an ever-changing volcanic landscape,” Rhonda Loh, then the park’s acting superintendent, said in January 2020.

A safer viewing area opened in March 2020, about 1,000 feet past the gate at the end of Chain of Craters Road and set back from the cliff edge.

Later that year, massive surf from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a chunk of rock from the lower part of the arch.

The park is urging visitors to stay back from the unstable cliffs, which drop vertically into the ocean and present a serious risk of falling.

After the collapse, photos on social media showed people entering the closed area near where the arch once stood.

According to the park, that puts both the visitors and first responders at great risk of falling and drowning off the rough, wave-swept coast.

Visitors are required to stay out of closed areas and away from cliff edges, which can collapse without warning.

The park describes individual sea arches as an ephemeral feature of the island’s constantly shifting coastline.

As the cliff slowly migrates inland, other arches will form and replace Hōlei, the park says. The park notes that erosion does not stop once an arch has formed.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s announcement of the collapse, its pages on Hōlei Sea Arch and how sea arches form, and its 2020 releases on the closure of the overlook and the new viewing area.

Space and time seem like the bedrock of reality. But startling clues are leading physicists toward the possibility that something stranger lies beneath.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every experience we have and every moment we live unfold naturally across space and time ‪—‬ so naturally that we rarely stop to question their existence.

Physics takes this just as much for granted as we do. For more than 100 years, the field has been built upon the foundational idea that space-time — the four-dimensional fabric of the universe — is fundamental.

But new insights drawn from the hearts of black holes, quantum computers and ultraprecise lasers, are now poised to challenge this assumption, leading a growing number of physicists to ask the same question: What if space and time aren't the bedrock of the universe, but emerge from something even deeper?

"You can build space from a theory without space," Jeff Forshaw, a professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester in the U.K., told Live Science.

For decades, we have known that two extraordinarily successful descriptions of nature are incompatible.

In Einstein's general theory of relativity, matter and energy bend space-time and we experience that curvature as gravity. Quantum mechanics, meanwhile, describes nature on the smallest scales of atoms and subatomic particles.

But quantum mechanics still has no adequate description of the force of gravity. The conflict between these theories of big and small becomes unavoidable in extreme environments, such as the centers of black holes or the smallest fractions of a second after the Big Bang, where gravity grows to be intense on the minute scales ruled by quantum mechanics.

An artist's illustration of the Big Bang with time running from the image's bottom to the top. During the first brief fraction of a second after the Big Bang the universe was so dense that quantum effects and gravity were equally strong.

So far, efforts to combine them mathematically and theoretically have led to nonsensical results.

"They seem not to fit together into a single, consistent framework that we know to be correct," Latham Boyle, a theoretical physicist at the University of Edinburgh in the U.K, told Live Science.

It's possible that one or both of these theories is incomplete, but an increasingly popular belief among physicists is that both theories are perched upon an untested assumption: space-time itself.

Both general relativity and quantum mechanics assume that space-time exists. Yet neither explains why our universe seems to have three dimensions of space and one of time, or where space-time comes from. If this assumption is wrong, the apparent foundation of reality could be a large-scale approximation of something even more mysterious.

In Einstein's model, space-time is a little like how people once viewed water: smooth and continuous, capable of bending and rippling. But water only appears continuous on large scales because we can't see its composite "bits," or individual molecules, said Boyle, whose research explores quantum gravity, the early universe and whether space-time is fundamental or emergent. One proposal is that space-time is similar.

"It seems smooth but only because we can't view it under a fine enough microscope," Boyle told Live Science. Yet no one has found direct evidence for space-time's microscopic "bits." That leaves physicists searching for indirect clues in places where existing theories are pushed to their breaking point: black holes.

At the hearts of black holes, general relativity breaks down by predicting space-time curving infinitely, while quantum physics gives their boundaries baffling properties.

Around black holes gravity (the curvature of space-time) is warped to an infinite degree.

Black holes also offer intriguing clues that space-time, like water, may have microscopic ingredients. One clue comes from thermodynamics ‪—‬ the laws governing heat, temperature and entropy.

Entropy is often described as measuring the disorder in a system, but physicists use it to describe how many hidden microscopic arrangements can produce the same large-scale behavior. A glass of water, for example, may have one temperature and pressure even though its molecules could be moving and arranged in an enormous number of different ways. The more possible microscopic arrangements there are, the greater its entropy.

This matters because thermodynamics usually describes the large-scale behavior of microscopic ingredients. If Einstein’s equations are thermodynamic in nature, their entropy may be due to hidden microscopic states of space-time that physicists cannot yet see.

"General relativity is thermodynamics," Forshaw said. "Einstein's equations are a statement of thermodynamics. They're a statistically emergent feature of an underlying theory."

In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking showed that black holes, too, have entropy and a physical temperature. This raised striking questions: Are there microscopic ingredients that account for those thermodynamic properties, and if so, what are they?

If those constituents exist, then space-time's smooth geometry, like the continuous appearance of water, emerges only on larger scales.

Another clue is that Einstein's equations appear to contain traces of this hidden structure, somehow reproducing the relationships needed for black holes to have a temperature, even though the theory directly connects the shape of space-time only to the matter it contains.

"Einstein's equation, which we thought was just a classical equation, nothing to do with quantum mechanics, seems to secretly know — or at some level to have known — about this finite entropy associated with the black hole," Boyle said.

The entropy of black holes also gives rise to a second sign that space-time emerges from something deeper: a puzzle known as the black hole information paradox.

Stephen Hawking in front of a projection of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula for black holes.

Quantum mechanics says that physical information can never be destroyed. Yet if black holes emit radiation — an idea famously proposed by Stephen Hawking in 1974 — they should slowly evaporate. This is a profound contradiction: A black hole's Hawking radiation is thermal, depending solely on its mass, electric charge and angular momentum. It contains no obvious record of what originally fell inside. That means that if the black hole eventually disappears, the information of what it once gobbled up seems to vanish with it.

But a black hole's entropy scales not with the three-dimensional volume enclosed by it but with the two-dimensional area of its event horizon, the point beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. Therefore, it's possible that all the information within any region might somehow be stored on its boundary. This became known as the holographic principle, named after a hologram, in which a 3D image is encoded on a 2D surface.

In 1997, theoretical physicist Juan Maldacena made the idea mathematically precise. He showed that a higher-dimensional theory containing gravity could be mapped onto a lower-dimensional quantum theory without it.

The two descriptions appeared to be interchangeable, equally valid views of reality. But some researchers now go further: They think the lower-dimensional quantum theory may be the fundamental description, while the higher-dimensional space-time we seem to live in is what emerges when its information is decoded.

These ideas gave rise to holography. Its central principle is that a gravitational world in more dimensions may be completely encoded by a quantum theory without gravity in fewer dimensions. That lower-dimensional theory lives on the boundary of the higher-dimensional spacetime.

You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real

Mark Van Raamsdonk, a professor of physics at the University of British Columbia, compares the concept to a computer's memory chip. At the fundamental level, a video game is encoded in physical bits switching between states. Yet on a screen, those bits produce a representation of a 3D world containing objects, movement and physical rules. The virtual world seems spatially real, even though its underlying information is stored very differently.

"You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real," Van Raamsdonk told Live Science.

Quantum entanglement may play a central role in how this lower-dimensional information gives rise to higher-dimensional space-time. It describes how particles can share linked quantum properties, even when separated by vast distances.

"If I want to decode what space-time geometry is being stored by the quantum state of this lower-dimensional system, all I need to do is probe this entanglement structure," Van Raamsdonk said.

For decades, directly testing this theory appeared hopeless. Physicists thought they would need particle collisions approaching the Planck scale — the fantastically high energy at which quantum effects are expected to become as important as gravity, and far beyond anything existing colliders can produce.

But physicists realized they don't need to rely on brute force. They are now developing several ways around that energy barrier.

The CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid) detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Reaching the Planck scale requires roughly 900 trillion times more energy than the Large Hadron Collider can produce.

How could scientists discover whether space-time has a deeper structure? One way is to search for a subtle jitter, or static hum, in space-time itself. Experiments such as GQuEST, a collaboration involving Fermilab and Caltech, and QUEST at Cardiff University in the U.K. split laser light along different paths and recombine it. Extraordinarily small changes in the distance light travels may reveal fluctuations, arising from discrete building blocks of space-time, that are consistent with some of holography's models.

In some holographic models, physicists represent the underlying units of information as quantum bits (qubits) — mathematically identical to those used in quantum computers. Physically, a computer qubit may be encoded in an ion or electrical circuit, whereas a qubit in a holographic model represents a possible microscopic unit of the quantum theory from which space-time emerges. This equivalence allows quantum processors to simulate space-time models.

In such models, the patterns of entanglement between the qubits dictate the physical distances between regions of space. The stronger those entanglements are, the closer together two corresponding regions are; if the entanglements are severed, the space-time between them tears apart.

QUEST compares measurements from two neighboring laser beam splitters, or interferometers. Some theoretical models predict quantum fluctuations of space-time that would affect both instruments in a related way. Researchers therefore search for matching fluctuations in their measurements while working to rule out shared sources of laboratory noise. Finding the predicted pattern could support those models; finding nothing would constrain how strong such fluctuations could be, killing off flawed models and refining how microscopic components (or chunks of information) translate into space-time's geometry.

Atom interferometers such as AION and MAGIS-100 extend the search for quantum jitters by using atoms as sensitive probes. When a laser pulse hits an atom, the atom enters superposition, in which it is simultaneously in two different locations at once. It then travels along two separate paths before being recombined by a final pulse. If space-time fluctuates slightly differently along one path than the other, a measurable shift is detected in the atom's interference pattern.

The cold-atom preparation and trapping apparatus for the strontium atom source in Fermilab's Matter-wave Atomic Gradiometer Interferometric Sensor (MAGIS-100).

Another approach called BMV experiments (after the surnames of their independent developers Sougato Bose and his collaborators, Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral) take diamond nanocrystals weighing around a hundred-billonth of a kilogram and place them into a state of quantum superposition.

Painstakingly shielded from every possible electromagnetic and nuclear interaction, and placed at different distances from one another, the diamonds are put through a key test. If they emerge from the experiment with the electron states entangled, then gravity alone produced the entanglement.

That would be evidence that gravity can transmit quantum effects — something a classical gravitational field could not produce. And if gravity (the curvature of space-time) can exist in superposition, it could be a strong clue that space-time's geometry is woven out of quantum information. The challenge, so far, is in excluding all the other effects that may obscure the signal.

On cosmic scales, future gravitational wave observatories ‪—‬ including the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer ‪—‬ could scrutinize gravity at the first clues' source: around black holes. After two black holes merge, the resulting object settles down by emitting gravitational waves with characteristic frequencies and decay times. Einstein's theory makes precise predictions for this "ringdown," allowing researchers to search for discrepancies.

An artist's illustration for how the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect ripples in space-time created by merging black holes.

Such discrepancies could potentially point to the quantum nature of space-time near black holes. Interpreting them would require distinguishing between competing explanations ‪—‬ an unexpected signal could cryptically hint at space-time's underlying nature, but it wouldn't reveal a direct picture of its microscopic ingredients.

To identify the bits that make up the reality beneath space-time, scientists are also turning to quantum computers. By entangling many qubits in specific ways to mimic different models of emergent space-time, scientists could determine which mathematical models of the constituent bits are more likely.

"The study of many-body, highly entangled systems is where the future of this whole enterprise is," Forshaw said.

Precursor tests are already underway. In 2022, for example, Google's Sycamore quantum processor was used to reproduce the behavior of a simple theoretical wormhole — not by creating a real hole in space-time but by arranging nine qubits so that their behavior could also be described using gravity.

Earlier this year, researchers went further, using the trapped-ion quantum computer IonQ Forte to test how something resembling gravitational geometry could emerge from patterns of quantum information. The qubits in Forte were arranged into a model that could be interpreted in two connected ways: both as a network of quantum information and as a simple holographic geometry. The researchers then altered the entanglement between the qubits. In the model’s gravitational interpretation, this was akin to adding mass. Just as adding mass bends Einstein's space-time, the researchers expected changing the entanglement to alter the corresponding geometry — and it did.

The findings demonstrate that researchers can study a mathematical relationship between entanglement and geometry using quantum hardware. However, they do not establish that our space-time emerges from lower-dimensional quantum information.

"The experiment that we did is a baby step in that direction," Crystal Noel, an experimental physicist at Duke University who led the experimental side of the project, told Live Science. One limitation of this result is that it reproduces features of a simplified, static theoretical universe, rather than the expanding universe in which we live. Testing a more realistic model of the universe might require entangling 100 or 200 qubits, which may be possible in the near future.

Each of these experiments will probe different aspects of the relationship between gravity and quantum physics, although none would by itself prove that space-time emerges from information. Taken together, however, their results could begin to reveal what theories of quantum gravity match the real world — and whether emergent space-time is among them.

Such a discovery would raise profound questions not only about the universe’s foundations, but about what it means for anything — including ourselves — to exist within it.

"If I tell you that space doesn't exist, it really questions what it means to be," Forshaw said. "How can you actually talk about things when there's no space to put things in?"

#6421. A one-in-a-million catch in a New York harbor turns out to be a bright yellow burbot

A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service crew caught a rare yellow burbot in Oswego Harbor, New York. A genetic condition gave it the color, and it went to Cornell.

Biologists with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service were running a routine survey in Oswego Harbor, New York, on Lake Ontario, in October when they pulled up a fish they did not expect. It was a burbot, and it was bright yellow-orange.

The agency calls it a one-in-a-million catch. The fish has xanthochromism, a rare condition that gives it a saturated yellow-orange color.

The agency said the fish would make even the brightest fall foliage look pale in comparison.

It is also the first burbot ever documented during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although a few anglers have reported catching them there.

Xanthochromism is caused by a genetic mutation that suppresses normal pigmentation and produces the yellow-orange appearance.

It is considerably less common in wild fish than albinism or melanism, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service. Unusual colors like this have surprised scientists before, as with a bright orange shark.

The place was a surprise too. Burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, and the species usually lives in deeper, cooler water than what is found inside the harbor.

The crew was not looking for burbot. It came from the Lower Great Lakes Fish and Wildlife Conservation Office, and it was carrying out an Aquatic Invasive Species survey.

The program watches harbors, rivers and bays of the Great Lakes for invasive species on a watchlist.

Because invaders are often rare when they first arrive, the crews use several methods at once, including electrofishing, fyke nets, gill nets and environmental DNA, or eDNA.

Invaders are an old problem in these waters: the Great Lakes have been under invasion from one species for 70 years.

Most fish caught in these surveys are native species. Catching a rare native fish suggests the program may also detect newly arriving invaders when their numbers are still very low.

The agency summed it up as an effective survey strategy, along with a bit of luck.

The burbot is a native fish of the Great Lakes. It tends to live on the lake bottom, and it is the only cod-like fish species in freshwater, according to a New York Sea Grant fact sheet. The same fact sheet calls it a formidable predator.

In the Great Lakes, sea lamprey predation has been a common factor affecting burbot numbers.

A 2006 study led by U.S. Geological Survey scientists found that burbot abundance in eastern Lake Erie increased significantly between 1987 and 2003.

The researchers, writing in Transactions of the American Fisheries Society, attributed the apparent recovery to effective sea lamprey control.

The same study suggested that a relatively high density of alewives, a small plankton-eating fish, probably held burbot numbers down in Lakes Ontario and Michigan at the time.

When U.S. Geological Survey fisheries biologists who know the species processed the yellow burbot, they noticed it was emaciated and looked to be in poor health.

Because of its condition, and because the reasons the species remains so scarce in the lake are still unexplained, the fish was sent to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis. The agency has not reported the results.

The agency says the catch could turn out to be lucky for the species too.

The rare fish may offer valuable insight into the health of burbot populations across the basin, and that could help guide how they are managed.

The information was obtained from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, a New York Sea Grant fact sheet and a U.S. Geological Survey study.

#6420. Two stars in the Andromeda galaxy merged before astronomers’ eyes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A star called “Little Bao” danced with its giant partner “Big Bao”

An image captured by NASA’s Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) telescope shows the Andromeda galaxy, which is the closest large galaxy to our Milky Way — and the home galaxy of Big and Little Bao.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

For seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Big Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.)

First, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

Instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Big Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

Still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

They’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”

#6419. The 8 Best Countertop Ice Makers for Pounds of Ice on Demand

These handy small appliances ensure there’s a continual supply of cubes to keep your drinks cold.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You may not think much about ice until you need it and are out. Many refrigerators offer a supply of crescent-shaped cubes with the push of a button, though built-in ice makers are prone to breaking and require upkeep. Filling up ice cube trays at the sink is often cumbersome, especially if you need large quantities of ice or don’t have extra freezer space.

Rather than rely on your fridge, a countertop ice maker churns out pounds of ice over 24 hours for soda, cocktails, and iced coffee. Some compact models are also handy for tailgating, RV trips, or car camping.

But like any small appliance, they have different attributes to consider to find a model that suits your needs, including size, capacity, water source connection, and features like LED lighting and a self-cleaning mode. Whether you’re looking for a kitchen or portable model, these are the best countertop ice makers we recommend to keep beverages cold, along with some advice on what to look out for as you make your pick.

To put together this list of the best countertop ice makers, we used our expert knowledge of the kitchen appliance space to narrow down our pool. Elizabeth Briskin—the original author of this guide—is a chef, recipe developer, and food writer who is all too familiar with the necessity of ice in the kitchen. She uses her own ice maker multiple times per day for tasks like shocking her delicate veggies after blanching them—this keeps them from continuing to cook and getting soggy.

For this latest update, we researched current brands and features and tested three new ice makers for ease of use, ice quality, and type. We also considered noise level, overall aesthetics, and speed, and we included models with a range of features (like ice cube sizes, draining ability, portability, and self-cleaning functions) at different price points.

This high-powered ice maker from Frigidaire is our top pick thanks to its thoughtful design, high output, compact size, and easy-to-use interface. It offers two sizes of bullet ice cubes—which are cylindrical with a rounded tip and hollow center—and the ice maker produces its first cubes in less than six minutes.

It holds up to 2.2 pounds of ice cubes at a time and produces up to 26 pounds per day, so it’s a good choice for larger households. The flip-up lid is transparent for seeing your supply straight away. As unused ice melts, the machine recycles the water to make fresh ice, saving you from draining it constantly.

Full Frigidaire EFIC189 Countertop Ice Maker Review

Whether you’re headed on a picnic, hosting an outdoor barbecue, or organizing an office party, this portable, lightweight machine provides all the conveniences and eliminates the hassle of hauling bags of ice. What’s more, it’s very affordable and easy to operate.

While many ice makers weigh over 20 pounds, this one is just shy of 13 and comes with a convenient carrying handle and insulated ice compartment. It produces up to 26 pounds of bullet-shaped ice per day, with the first cubes ready in as quickly as six minutes. A self-cleaning function keeps ice fresh.

Nothing beats the chewy crunch of nugget ice, and having the GE Profile Opal 2.0 Ultra Nugget ice maker on your counter means you’ll have a steady supply. The Opal 2.0 Ultra produces ice faster than the original version, taking just 10 minutes to complete its first batch versus 15.

The side tank holds ¾ gallons of water, so you can basically turn it on and forget about it—until you’re ready for a new drink, that is. Simply open the door, and use the scoop to remove what you need. There’s also an XL version of the side tank that holds a gallon of water.

We like that this ice maker has a large capacity for making and holding ice. It churns out up to 38 pounds per day, and the ice basket holds up to 3 pounds. The scale inhibiting filter keeps the machine cleaner for longer, and the advanced cleaning system the ice maker sanitizes and descales itself when it’s used regularly. When it is time to clean it, just activate the self-cleaning mode.

We did notice during our testing that this model does some noticeable noise when operating and it does take up a bit of counter space. However, these cons proved to be minor inconveniences, as this model truly is a solid workhorse for nugget ice.

Full GE Profile Opal 2.0 Ultra Nugget Ice Maker Review

Ideal for kitchens tight on space (i.e. dorm and RVs), this aqua ice maker from Igloo’s Nostalgia line is a reliable, budget-friendly pick that adds a fun pop of color wherever you choose to use it. It churns out 26 pounds of ice in 24 hours, with nine cubes ready in just about seven minutes.

It offers two cube sizes—a handy feature for the price—and the removable basket holds up to 1.25 pounds of ice at a time. A drain plug makes cleanup simple, while the carry handle makes it portable for picnics or RV trips. While it does require frequent refills and the fan is a bit noisy, its vintage design and above-average features for the price make it a reliable, stylish choice.

A standout for home mixologists and party hosts alike, the Luma Countertop Ice Maker produces up to 40 pounds of crystal-clear, restaurant-quality ice daily. Its innovative process freezes water in layers to eliminate impurities, creating ice that melts slowly, keeps drinks balanced, and reduces fizz in cocktails and spirits. Extra-thick insulation keeps ice colder for longer, with melted ice recycled for the next batch.

A simple one-button operation and adjustable thickness setting make it ideal for a variety of cocktails, from Juleps to Negronis. Though it’s a bit bulkier than others and takes a bit longer per batch, it produces more, better-quality ice, making the first cubes in 15 minutes.

Our tester loved how quickly this machine made soft nugget ice—it only took about 6 minutes per batch. All you have to do is fill the water tank and turn the machine on to get things started. The LED interior light is a great added feature because you’re able to see the ice as it’s being made, and it adds a fun design touch as it sits on the countertop.

We appreciate that the front drawer makes it easy to access ice as soon as a cycle finishes, and the machine produces up to 40 pounds per day. This model includes a self-cleaning feature to keep the machine fresh, and the bottom drain allows you to swiftly empty the reservoir tank before storing the unit.

If you’ve ever gotten a craft cocktail at a restaurant and wanted to recreate it at home, giant ice cube and all, this is the ice machine for you. The Klaris Clear Ice Maker creates four crystal clear, slow-melting ice cubes that are 2 inches square. We like that the machine is compact and fits nicely on the countertop while taking up minimal cabinet or closet space if you need to store it away for any reason. The clear cubes, meanwhile, elevate craft cocktails, mocktails, iced coffee, or just a big glass of water.

While the ice does take up to 12 hours to make, there is a delay start option, which allows you to time ice production cycles to accommodate your schedule. Our tester mistimed the first batch, and the cubes that had formed overnight were melted by the morning. Using the delay start feature helps avoid this. You also have the option to purchase custom storage containers that hold four cubes each, so you have craft ice at the ready for your next cocktail party.

Whether you want small or large ice cubes for your favorite beverages, the Kenmore Top Load Ice Maker delivers both, making it a strong first foray into ice makers if you’re still on the fence. This machine makes nine bullet-shaped cubes in about seven minutes, and there are two different sizes to choose from. The top-load design and included scoop make grabbing ice a breeze.

This model comes with a carrying handle, making it a more portable option than other countertop ice makers we’ve tried. The self-cleaning mode and bottom drain allow for more simplified maintenance. You need to let it sit upright for 24 hours before your first use, so make sure you account for that before you need your ice.

Consider your ice cube style preference when deciding on a countertop ice maker. Most machines do not pop out the crystal-clear ice you’d find at a top-tier restaurant or bar. Instead, some of the most popular shapes are nugget ice cubes, also known as pellets or Sonic. Soft and chewable, this style is the cube of choice at restaurants like Sonic and Chick-fil-A, but the cubes melt quickly, and the machines that make them tend to be more expensive due to their popularity. Also, consider if you’ll want different ice sizes for different drinks. Many machines offer two cube sizes—a smaller one good for sodas and iced coffees and a larger option more suited for cocktails. If you plan to make both, look for one of these.

There isn’t much of a difference in size among the best countertop ice makers. Some space-savers are tall and narrow, while others are lower and deep, ideal to fit beneath a kitchen cabinet. At most, countertop ice makers range from roughly 10 to 15 inches deep and 12 to 17 inches high.

Most countertop ice makers designed for kitchens produce 26 pounds of ice in 24 hours. This is more than enough for households with four to six people, assuming there are no major ice demands (like a party). Larger households or offices may appreciate a more productive machine that churns out 30 or more pounds of ice per day.

Countertop ice makers either use water from a built-in reservoir or a connected water line, but the former is most common. You’ll need to refill a reservoir ice maker with water when it runs out. The major benefit is it doesn’t require any plumbing connections—you just fill the tank and it’s ready to use. Just keep in mind that most machines recommend using filtered water to prevent mineral deposits from building up.

If your ice maker will be running all the time and you don’t want to hear constant humming and clinking, look for a model that produces 40 decibels of sound or less. Some ice makers automatically run when they sense the basket is running low on ice—keep this in mind if you prefer a quieter machine.

Self-cleaning is an important feature to consider and look for, as cleaning a countertop ice maker requires dumping ice and removing and replacing several components. With a simple click of a button, you know your machine is clean and the ice tastes fresh. After all, using the best quality ice amplifies the taste of your beverages, too.

Yes, whether you hook your ice maker up to a water line or use a refillable tank, you can keep it supplied with tap water. However, if you find that your tap water has an unpleasant flavor, you may prefer to use filtered water.

Yes, it’s perfectly safe to leave most ice makers on during the day and night. Of course, if you’re not using the ice, you will be using electricity to keep it running.

Some countertop ice makers require a water hookup. This means you’ll need to place the machine near some plumbing in your kitchen. If this isn’t an option for your home, however, many of the machines we love use a refillable water reservoir instead of, or in addition to, a water line.

#6418. A peanut by a lamp can make a city crow warier than a passing human

With a lamp base beside the peanuts, feeding odds fell to 0.53 for city crows and 0.76 for country crows in a Binghamton study of 20 crow families.

In 2019 and 2020, a team led by biologist Dave J. Colucci put out peanuts in the shell for 20 families of American crows around Ithaca, New York. Ten families lived in town, and ten in farm fields and natural areas of the nearby Town of Dryden.

On some mornings the peanuts had company: a rock, an ear of corn in its husk, a paper takeout box or a faux-wood lamp base. Country crows held back more around the box, and city crows around the corn.

City crows were also less likely to eat next to the lamp, the study by Colucci and Anne Clark of Binghamton University found. Other urban-rural differences in the paper had only weak support.

Colucci earned a PhD at Binghamton in 2025. Clark is an associate professor emerita of biological sciences there, the Binghamton University release of November 16, 2026, says. The paper came out online in Behavioral Ecology on October 22.

Each family’s territory got a feeding spot. The bait was 2 cups of raw, unsalted peanuts in a circle about 3 feet (1 meter) wide. They picked spots with little human traffic and no sign of predators or competitors.

In town these were parking lots, dead-end streets and parks in Ithaca, Lansing and Cayuga Heights. Out in Dryden the sites were on private or public land.

Each family got three days with peanuts only and four days with an object, 140 trials in total, each starting between 6 and 8 a.m.

A hidden camcorder sat at least 10 feet (3 meters) from the bait. The observer stayed 164 feet (50 meters) or more away.

The team ranked the objects by how often a crow in each place would have seen them. Rocks are everywhere and corn grows in Dryden, while takeout boxes are more common in town.

“What we wanted to show was that aversion would decrease with the amount of experience that we expected our crow to have had with these objects,” Colucci said in the release.

To test the trash part, the team surveyed a 1-mile (1.61-kilometer) road route in each area weekly for three weeks. They counted 341 human-made objects, 169 in town and 172 in the country. Rural ones stayed put longer, 2.81 weeks on average against 2.27.

The box cut feeding more for rural crows and the corn cut it more for urban crows. But the paper says the evidence for that switch was limited.

Crows that live near an Arby’s or a McDonald’s learn to recognize that chain’s boxes, Clark said in the release. The box in the test was a plain one with no brand.

The lamp base was supposed to be new to every crow, in town or out. The authors chose it because it has none of the usual signs of a human-made thing, like bright colors, shine or sharp corners.

With peanuts alone, nearly every visit ended in feeding, a probability of 0.99 in town and 0.97 in Dryden. Put the lamp down and it fell to 0.53 for urban crows and 0.76 for rural crows, according to the paper’s Bayesian model.

How fast the birds came in was another matter. Timing for the boldest crow in each family was about the same in both places with the lamp out. That held for reaching 10 feet (3 meters) of the bait and for taking a first peanut.

Overall, the urban families did reach the bait sooner, at 4.23 times the rural rate. The authors attribute this to the rural crows partly reacting to the person on watch, since country crows are warier of people.

Earlier work had mostly found that city birds are bolder with new things, which is why the release calls this somewhat surprising. Clark said urban crows “are social animals” that watch one another. “In an area that has a lot of new opportunities, there are also new threats,” she said.

The second test was about people. An experimenter walked toward single crows and noted how close the walker got before each one flew, a figure biologists call flight initiation distance.

One person did all 145 trials, in upstate New York and in Quebec, in 2019, 2022 and 2023. The pace was a steady 2.7 miles per hour (1.2 meters per second). On some walks the experimenter looked at the crow, and on others tilted the whole face down.

On average the crows took off when the walker was about 149 feet (45.3 meters) away. The walker got closer than 33 feet (10 meters) only 8 times. Where the walker looked mattered only in more crowded places.

The model looked at areas with about 13,000 people per square mile (5,000 per square kilometer). There, it put the distance for a downward look near zero, about 82 feet (25 meters) shorter than for a stare. Rural crows left at about the same distance either way.

The authors warn that those predictions are uncertain. Human population within about half a mile (800 meters) of each trial predicted flight distance best.

Crow hunting is allowed in rural New York in a set season but prohibited within city limits, the paper notes. The release says crows, seen as a nuisance, are more likely to be shot in rural areas.

Clark called the rural behavior “a blunt, anti-predator strategy” in the release. “Whereas in urban areas, if you were fleeing at every human, you’d never spend any time on the ground,” she said.

The authors compare the gaze result with earlier work on Seattle crows, where flight distance was on average about 10.5 feet (3.2 meters) shorter for an indirect gaze.

Separate University of Washington mask experiments found that wild crows learned the faces of dangerous people and passed the details to other crows. They remembered a threatening person for up to 17 years.

Separate lab work in Germany found carrion crows that made decisions about twice as fast as humans in a visual task.

The town sites were really suburban, the authors say, not downtown. The litter count covered roadsides at one site per area, and the timing data on approaches came from 2020 only.

One person ran every flight trial, and the approach timings may partly reflect wariness of the experimenter. Census numbers may also miss parks and shopping areas, where few people live but many walk through.

The lamp may not have been fully new to city crows either. It is perfectly symmetrical around its vertical axis, a shape rare in nature and common in things people make. So the town-country gap could be underestimated, the paper says.

In Ithaca and Dryden, the 20 crow families got the same peanuts. What sat next to them, and who was walking by, changed what they did.

The full study was published in the journal Behavioral Ecology.
